media.title: Mat Weaver
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Mat Weaver
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M1.S1.T1.C2.2D1
- Tool type: Exploration (the free first try of the chapter; the video that follows names how to say a row in words)
- Textbook source: Shapes and Patterns, Weaving Mats, the paper-mat activity (a strip going 1 under and 1 over, the next strip 1 over and 1 under, all strips alternating) and the sentence "We can describe the pattern of the above weave as follows" (developer only). Practice values: 8 slits, and the rule 2 over, 2 under.
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student sees that a weave is made by a strip going over and under, that the next strip does the opposite, and can say Row 1 and Row 2 of their own mat in words.
- Out of scope: counting rows until a pattern repeats, moving a row along, "do not repeat" steps, long rules (all in the next tool).
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- A close-up top view of a pale wooden desk. In the middle lies a leaf-green paper mat with 8 upright slits, drawn as photo-style paper with a soft shadow; it is the largest thing on the stage (about 60% of its width). A small photo of a woven basket sits in the top-left corner of the desk. Under the mat a tray holds 8 paper strips, 4 blue and 4 yellow, each longer than the mat is wide.
- The first blue strip lies across Row 1. Where it crosses the 8 slits there are 8 round dotted rings (the crossings), numbered 1 to 8 above the mat.
- Instruction line: "Tap a crossing to make the strip go over or under."
- The first ring pulses once, inviting the child to tap it.
2. Scene and Objects
- Mat: 8 slits across and 8 rows down, one row for each strip, with row numbers 1 to 8 on the left edge. A strip that is "over" at a crossing shows its colour on top of the green paper; "under" hides it below a green band with a small shadow.
- Tray: strips in the order blue, yellow, blue, yellow, and so on; each strip leaving the tray lands across the next free row. Counter under the tray: "strips woven 2 of 8".
- Row read-out: one thin line under the mat that says the row in words as it is woven, for example "Row 1: 1 under, 1 over, 1 under, 1 over, ... (repeat)". "(repeat)" is added once the same group has come twice.
- Goal chip in the top corner of the stage, for example "Row 1". Bottom buttons (large, three only): Hint, Reset, Next. Next is locked until the goal chip is green.
3. Main Interaction
- Tap a ring: the strip goes over there (colour shows). Tap again: under (colour hides). Tap again: over, and so on. The row read-out grows from left to right. A strip is finished when all 8 crossings are set; tapping the tray then brings the next strip. A finished strip is locked. Reset clears the mat and brings all 8 strips back.
- Rows below are written with O for over and U for under, from slit 1 to slit 8.
- Activity 4 only: a round button "Weave the next strip" on the tray weaves the next strip as the opposite of the strip above, with a small slide animation.
- Star challenge only: word cards appear under the mat: the number cards 1, 2, 3 and 4, the cards "over" and "under" and the card "(repeat)". Tap cards to build a sentence; tap the last card again to remove it.
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Weave the blue strip: 1 under, then 1 over, again and again." Goal chip: "Row 1". Setup: blue strip across Row 1, 8 empty rings. Help: guided, a ghost word under the next ring says "under" or "over" in turn. Guess: before the first tap, two cards ask where the strip will show on top: "Top at slits 1, 3, 5, 7" or "Top at slits 2, 4, 6, 8". Result: the strip is woven UOUOUOUO; the right card turns green with a gentle bounce. Why line: "The strip goes under slit 1 and over slit 2, so it shows on top at slits 2, 4, 6 and 8: 4 + 4 = 8 slits."
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Weave the yellow strip across Row 2: 1 over, then 1 under." Goal chip: "Row 2". Help: guided, ghost words as before. Guess: "Will Row 2 go over where Row 1 goes over?" with cards "Yes, the same" and "No, the opposite". Result: the strip is woven OUOUOUOU and the mat starts to show small squares. Why line: "Row 2 goes over where Row 1 goes under, so it shows on top at slits 1, 3, 5 and 7."
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "Guess Row 3, then weave it." Goal chip: "Row 3". Setup: blue strip across Row 3, no ghost words. Guess: cards "Like Row 1", "Like Row 2" and "A new pattern". Result: Row 3 is UOUOUOUO. Why line: "Row 2 swapped Row 1. Swap Row 2 and you get Row 1 back: 1 under, 1 over, 1 under, 1 over, ... (repeat)." Help: independent.
- Activity 4 (independent). Goal line: "Weave the rest of the mat." Goal chip: "8 strips". Setup: strips 1 to 3 woven, 5 in the tray. Guess: "How many blue strips will the whole mat have?" with cards 3, 4 and 5. The child presses the round button 5 times. Result: rows 1, 3, 5 and 7 are blue, rows 2, 4, 6 and 8 are yellow, and the mat shows a small check pattern. Why line: "4 blue and 4 yellow: 4 + 4 = 8 strips." Help: independent.
- Activity 5 (independent, practice values). Goal line: "Press Reset. Weave Row 1 with 2 over, 2 under, again and again. Then weave Row 2 by swapping." Goal chips: "Row 1", then "Row 2". Setup: a clear mat. Guess: "On how many slits will Row 1 show on top?" with cards 2, 4 and 6. Result: Row 1 is OOUUOOUU (shows on 4 slits) and Row 2 is UUOOUUOO. Why line: "2 over and 2 under make 4 slits, and 4 + 4 = 8, so the group comes 2 times. Row 2 swaps every over and under." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1. Goal line: "We can describe the pattern of the above weave as follows. Weave your own mat and say Row 1 and Row 2 in words." Goal chip: "Describe the weave". Setup: a clear mat; the child weaves 2 rows with a rule of their own (for example the rule of Activity 1 or 5). Guess: before weaving Row 2, the child taps what its first step will be, "over" or "under". The word cards then appear and the child builds a sentence for Row 1 and one for Row 2, for example "1 under, 1 over, (repeat)". Result: the tool expands each sentence to 8 slits and lays it over the woven row; a match turns the chip green and the read-out shows both rows. Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- Tapping over and under, the child sees that a strip is a list of over and under steps, that Row 2 does the opposite of Row 1, and that a few words ("1 under, 1 over, repeat") say a whole row.
- Rules in the child's words: "Over means the strip shows on top. Under means it goes below." "The next row can do the opposite." "Count the steps, then say repeat."
6. Feedback and Hints
- Wrong answer: red strip, a small shake of the object, and one friendly line naming the mistake and what to look at. No scores; trying again is always free. Correct: the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce, the pill gets a tick, and Next unlocks.
- Strip copies the row above -> "This strip goes over where the strip above goes over. Look again: should this row swap?" The copying crossings pulse.
- Row 1 starts with over -> "Row 1 starts with under: 1 under, then 1 over." Ring 1 pulses.
- Two overs or two unders side by side in Activities 1 to 3 -> "Two overs are side by side here. This rule goes over, under, over, under: look at slit 3." The two rings pulse.
- Strip never goes under -> "This strip never goes under, so it is not woven in. Try an under." All rings pulse once.
- Words that do not match the row -> "Count the steps that stay together, then say repeat." The row shows numbers under its steps and a bracket round each group.
- Hint button, 3 levels. (1) Words: "Does the strip lie on top, or go below, at the next slit?" (2) Visual clue: the next ring glows with a ghost "over" or "under". (3) Almost the answer: "Tap slit 1 for under, slit 2 for over, then keep going: under, over, under, over."
- Edge cases: an empty ring keeps the strip open ("One crossing is still empty: slit 6."); a tap on a locked strip shakes it ("That strip is fixed. Press Reset to start again."); in Activity 5 the groups end exactly at slit 8.
7. Ending
- The star challenge is done when both rows match their words; the end screen follows when all chips are green.
- End screen: confetti once. "Well done!" Remember: "Over means the strip shows on top. Under means it goes below." "The next row does the opposite of the row above." "Count the steps, then say repeat." Think and talk: "If you weave 8 rows like this, how many rows look the same as Row 1?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Images: pale wooden desk top view (photo); leaf-green paper mat with 8 slits (photo-style); blue and yellow paper strips (photo cut-outs); small woven basket photo. Rings, numbers and word cards are code-drawn. No people. English only.

tool_config.idea: Feel what over and under mean by weaving paper strips across a mat with slits, and see that the words for a row come from what you wove: 1 under, 1 over, repeat, and the next row swaps. This is the free first try of the chapter, so it asks and shows; the video that follows names how to describe a row in words.
tool_config.title: Mat Weaver
tool_config.screen: The craft table, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. A coloured paper mat with 8 upright slits (practice values) lies in the middle of the table and is the largest thing on screen. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. To the right of the mat a tray holds the 8 paper strips of your maths book, 4 blue and 4 yellow, each one longer than the mat is wide. The strip in hand lies across the first free row of the mat, and every place where it crosses a slit is a round tap spot. Controls: tap a crossing to switch it between over (the strip lies on top and shows its colour) and under (the strip goes below the slit paper and hides); an Alternate button that sets the whole strip to 1 under, 1 over, and so on; a Next strip button that fixes the strip and brings the next one from the tray; Undo, Hint, Retry (clears the strip in hand), Reset (clears the mat), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: a row read-out in words under the mat that grows as the strip is woven, for example Row 1: 1 under, 1 over, 1 under, 1 over, ... (repeat), with the word repeat added once the same group has come twice; a counter strips woven out of 8; and a card number out of 6.
feedback: Tapping a crossing slides the strip over or under with a gentle movement, and the row read-out adds the step in words.
A second strip that does the opposite of the row above gets a soft green note: This strip goes over where the last one goes under: the rows swap.
A strip that copies the row above gets a soft amber note: This strip goes over where the strip above goes over. Look again: should this row swap?
Alternate fills a strip with the pattern and says: 1 under, 1 over, again and again. Read the words in the read-out.
When the student describes a row that does not match the read-out, the tool shows the row with each step numbered and says: Count the steps that stay together. It never shows a red cross.
tool_config.done_when: Strips 1 and 2 are woven with the rows swapped, all 8 strips are woven, the student has woven and read a row of their own rule, and has described Row 1 and Row 2 of their own mat in words.

placement.where: last concept of the topic, after its teaching and worked examples

challenges: Card 1: weave strip 1 across the 8 slits going 1 under and 1 over, again and again. Read the row read-out. Answer: the strip goes under slit 1, over slit 2, under slit 3, over slit 4, and so on, so it goes over slits 2, 4, 6 and 8: 4 overs and 4 unders, and 4 + 4 = 8 slits. The read-out says Row 1: 1 under, 1 over, 1 under, 1 over, ... (repeat).

Card 2: weave strip 2 across the next row going 1 over and 1 under, again and again. Compare it with the row above. Answer: strip 2 goes over slits 1, 3, 5 and 7, and the read-out says Row 2: 1 over, 1 under, 1 over, 1 under, ... (repeat). Row 2 does the opposite of Row 1: where Row 1 goes over, Row 2 goes under.

Card 3: guess first. What will Row 3 be if it swaps over and under in Row 2? Tap your guess, then weave strip 3. Answer: Row 3 is the same as Row 1, because swapping Row 1 gave Row 2 and swapping Row 2 gives Row 1 back: 1 under, 1 over, 1 under, 1 over, ... (repeat).

Card 4: press Alternate to weave strips 4 to 8, each strip doing the opposite of the strip above. How many strips are blue and how many are yellow? Answer: 4 blue and 4 yellow, because 4 + 4 = 8 strips. The odd rows go like Row 1 and the even rows go like Row 2, so the mat shows small checks.

Card 5 (practice values): press Reset. Weave Row 1 with a rule of your own: 2 over, 1 under, again and again, then weave Row 2 by swapping over and under. Answer: Row 1: 2 over, 1 under, 2 over, 1 under, ... (repeat) goes over, over, under, over, over, under, over, over across the 8 slits. Row 2 swaps it: 2 under, 1 over, 2 under, 1 over, ... (repeat).

Challenge: 'We can describe the pattern of the above weave as follows.' Weave your own mat, then describe Row 1 and Row 2 in words. Answer: for the mat woven with 1 under and 1 over, Row 1: 1 under, 1 over, 1 under, 1 over, ... (repeat) and Row 2: 1 over, 1 under, 1 over, 1 under, ... (repeat). A rule of your own is fine too, if the words match what you wove. Your words may differ.

hint_ladder.text: What does the strip in hand do at each slit: does it lie on top, or go below the slit paper? Look at the first crossing and tap it.
Go slit by slit. For Row 1 the strip goes under, then over, then under, then over. Say the steps out loud as you tap.
For Row 1 tap slit 1 for under, slit 2 for over, slit 3 for under, and keep going to slit 8. The read-out should say 1 under, 1 over, ... (repeat).
Press Alternate. The strip weaves itself: under, over, under, over across the 8 slits. Now read the read-out and say the row in your own words.

student_does: Think back to the woven baskets of the story, each one with its own weaving pattern. Look at the paper mat with 8 slits and the strip in hand. Tap one crossing twice to see the strip go over (it shows on top) and then under (it hides), then press Next.

Weave strip 1 going 1 under and 1 over, weave strip 2 going 1 over and 1 under, guess Row 3 before you weave it, press Alternate to finish all 8 strips, then press Reset and try a rule of your own (practice values: 2 over, 1 under).
Answer the open question of the story. Weave your own mat and describe Row 1 and Row 2 in words, as your maths book does.

media.title: Weave Rules
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Weave Rules
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M1.S2.T2.C5.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity (build rows from rule tags, then find where the pattern repeats)
- Textbook source: Shapes and Patterns, Weaving Mats, questions 2, 3 and 4 and the "Let Us Try" grid design (developer only). Book numbers: 2 over, 1 under on 8 slits; four rules on 16 slits; two designs (16 slits and 11 slits); a 21 by 21 design. Practice values: 12 slits and the rule 3 over, 1 under.
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student builds the rows of a weave from rules made of counts of over and under steps with repeat, and finds the row where the pattern starts to repeat.
- Out of scope: more than 2 strip colours, and anything about turning or flipping a pattern.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- A wooden picture-frame loom seen from above (photo-style) with 12 pale vertical threads and a row of 12 empty crossings under a rule bar (a wooden bar with slots). Under the frame a tray holds wooden tags with white writing: 1, 2, 3, 4, "over", "under", "(repeat)" and "(do not repeat)".
- Instruction line: "Build Row 1 from the tags: 3 over, 1 under, then repeat." The tag "3" glows and the first slot pulses.
2. Scene and Objects
- Loom frame: the largest object, up to 16 threads across (12, 8, 16 or 11, set by the activity) and 8 rows down. "Over" shows a blue strip piece on top of the thread; "under" shows only the thread. Rows below are written O (over) and U (under).
- Rule bar above the row being built; a number tag and a word tag side by side make one step, for example "3 over". Slit counter on the bar ("12 of 12 slits"). Each woven row gets a small label of its words at its left end.
- Target card: a postcard clipped to the top-right corner when a mat is to be copied.
- On-stage round buttons (shown only when needed): "Weave", "Repeat these rows", "Rows repeat from here". Goal chip, for example "Row 1". Bottom buttons (large, three only): Hint, Reset, Next.
3. Main Interaction
- Drag tags into the slots in order. "(repeat)" goes last: do the steps after the last "(do not repeat)" tag again and again until the row is full. "(do not repeat)" goes right after a step done once at the start. Drag a tag out to remove it. "Weave" colours the row and adds its words to the row list; a rule that runs past the last thread is cut at the edge.
- Slide route (Activity 3): drag the ghost copy of the row above to the right, one slit at a time; the last step comes round to the front.
- "Repeat these rows" copies the rows built so far down the frame in order, up to 8 rows. Tap a row, then "Rows repeat from here", to mark the first row that is the same as Row 1. A colour dot at the end of each row switches blue and yellow (either is accepted).
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Build Row 1 from the tags: 3 over, 1 under, then repeat." Goal chip: "Row 1". Setup: 12 threads. Help: guided, each tag shows its slits. Guess: "How many slits will go under?" with cards 1, 3 and 6. Result: OOOUOOOUOOOU. Why line: "3 over and 1 under make 4 slits, and 4 + 4 + 4 = 12, so the group comes 3 times: 9 slits go over and 3 go under."
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Now build Row 2. It swaps over and under in Row 1." Goal chip: "Row 2". Help: guided, Row 1 stays as a pale ghost under the rule bar. Guess: "Row 2 starts with:" cards "over" and "under". Result: UUUOUUUOUUUO. Why line: "Where Row 1 goes over, Row 2 goes under: 3 under, 1 over, then repeat."
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "Slide Row 1 one slit to the right to make Row 2, and keep sliding to make Rows 3, 4 and 5. Which row looks like Row 1?" Goal chip: "Find the repeat". Setup: Row 1 (3 over, 1 under, repeat) is woven. Guess: "The rows will repeat after:" cards 3 rows, 4 rows and 5 rows. Result: the last step comes round to the front each time: Row 2 is UOOOUOOOUOOO, Row 3 is OUOOOUOOOUOO, Row 4 is OOUOOOUOOOUO, and Row 5 is the same as Row 1 (OOOUOOOUOOOU); the child taps Row 5 and "Rows repeat from here". Why line: "Row 5 is the same as Row 1, so the rows repeat after 4 rows." Help: independent, no ghost.
- Star Challenge 1. Goal line: "Can you figure out how to make this mat? Row 1: 2 over, 1 under, 2 over, 1 under, ... Row 2: 2 under, 1 over, 2 under, 1 over, ..." Goal chip: "Make the mat". Setup: 8 threads; the target card shows the blue and cream 8 by 8 mat. Guess: "Row 3 will look like:" cards "Row 1", "Row 2" and "A new row". The child builds Rows 1 and 2, then presses "Repeat these rows". Result: Rows 1, 3, 5 and 7 are OOUOOUOO, Rows 2, 4, 6 and 8 are UUOUUOUU, and the frame matches the target. Why line: "Row 2 swaps Row 1, and the two rows repeat down the mat: 2 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 2 = 8 slits." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 2. Goal line: "Try to weave a pattern, using the rules given below. Row 1: 2 over, 1 under, 2 over, 1 under, ... (repeat). Row 2: 1 under (do not repeat), 3 over, 3 under, 3 over, 3 under, ... (repeat). Row 3: 2 under, 1 over, 2 under, ... (repeat). Row 4: 1 over (do not repeat), 3 under, 3 over, ... (repeat). Continue weaving in this order." Goal chip: "Weave 4 rows". Setup: 16 threads; the target card shows the red and green mat. Guess: "Row 5 will look like:" cards "Row 1", "Row 4" and "A new row". The child builds Rows 1 to 4, presses "Repeat these rows", taps Row 5 and "Rows repeat from here". Result: Row 1 OOUOOUOOUOOUOOUO, Row 2 UOOOUUUOOOUUUOOO, Row 3 UUOUUOUUOUUOUUOU, Row 4 OUUUOOOUUUOOOUUU (Rows 3 and 4 swap Rows 1 and 2). Why line: "Row 5 follows the first rule again, so it is the same as Row 1: the pattern repeats after 4 rows." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 3. Goal line: "Can you work out the steps for any of these designs and weave the pattern? Write the steps of the pattern for each row until it starts repeating." Goal chip: "Find the repeat". Setup: the target card shows two designs; the child taps one, purple and light blue (16 threads) or teal and lavender (11 threads). Guess: "This design repeats after:" cards 3 rows, 4 rows and 6 rows. The child builds each row from tags in order (the row list is the notebook) and taps the row that matches Row 1. Rows expected, purple: UOOOUUUOOOUUUOOO, OOOUUUOOOUUUOOOU, OOUUUOOOUUUOOOUU, UUOOOUUUOOOUUUOO, UUUOOOUUUOOOUUUO, OUUUOOOUUUOOOUUU, then Row 7 is the same as Row 1 (repeats after 6 rows). Teal: OUUUOUUUOUU, OOUOOOUOOOU, UOOOUOOOUOO, UUOUUUOUUUO, then Row 5 is the same as Row 1 (repeats after 4 rows). Either design is accepted. Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 4. Goal line: "Draw the following pattern on a grid paper. Part of it is done for you. Now, complete the rest of the grid to get the full design." Goal chip: "Complete the design". Setup: a grid of 21 by 21 cells replaces the frame, with the green and yellow target mat beside it. Done for you: 36 yellow squares: 11 in row 1, then 2, 3 and 4 in rows 2 to 4, then 4 in each of rows 5 to 8. Guess: "The bottom row will have:" cards "11 squares, like the top row", "10 squares" and "5 squares". The child taps a cell to paint it yellow (again to clear) or drags along a diagonal to paint a run. The switch "Mirror" (on at the start) paints the matching cell on the other side of the middle column too. Result: 144 yellow squares; rows 1 and 21 have 11 each; the left half matches the right half. Why line: "The left half and the right half match, so draw one half and copy it." Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- A woven row is over and under steps written with counts and the word repeat. Writing rows one after the other, the child sees each differ a little from the one above, until a row is the same as Row 1.
- Rule in the child's words: "Write the rows until one is the same as Row 1. Then the pattern repeats."
6. Feedback and Hints
- Wrong answer: red strip, a small shake of the object, and one friendly line naming the mistake and what to look at. No scores; trying again is always free. Correct: the row slides into place, the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce, the pill gets a tick and Next unlocks.
- Row does not fill the slits -> "Your row covers 9 of 12 slits: one more step is needed." The slit counter pulses. Missing "(repeat)" -> "Add the tag (repeat) so the steps come again and again." The tag pulses.
- Copies the row above instead of moving it -> "Each new row can begin at a different place. Compare where the first group starts." The two first groups glow.
- "Rows repeat from here" on a row that is not the same as Row 1 -> the first slit that differs pulses and the line says "Not the same as Row 1 yet. Move on to the next row."
- Hint button, 3 levels. (1) Words: "How many slits does each step cover, and does the strip go over or under?" (2) Visual clue: the slits of the next step glow. (3) Almost the answer: the tool places the first two steps.
- Edge cases: a rule that runs past the last thread is cut ("The last group is cut at the edge: that is fine."); in Star Challenge 4 the squares sit on every other cell except in the middle, where rows 10, 11 and 12 hold runs of 3, 5 and 3 squares in a row.
7. Ending
- A star challenge is done when its result in section 4 is reached; the end screen follows when all chips are green.
- End screen: confetti once. "Well done!" Remember: "Write a row as counts of over and under, then say repeat." "Move a row along to make the next row." "When a row matches Row 1, the pattern repeats." Think and talk: "A weave repeats after 6 rows. What will Row 13 look like?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Images: wooden picture-frame loom with pale threads, blue and yellow strip pieces, wooden tags, paper postcard (photo cut-outs). Target mats and grids are code-drawn from the rows. English only.

tool_config.idea: Build the rows of a weave from rule cards (a count, over or under, repeat) and find the row where the pattern starts to repeat. The cards make the rule itself the thing that students handle, so long rules and many rows are quick to try.
tool_config.title: Weave Rules
tool_config.screen: A weaving frame with 16 columns on the craft table, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. The grid of crossings, 16 columns wide, is the largest thing on screen: in each row a crossing shows the strip colour where the strip goes over and cream where it goes under. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Above each row sits a rule line where cards are dropped in order. A shelf under the frame holds the rule cards: the number cards 1, 2 and 3, the word cards over and under, a card (repeat) and a card (do not repeat). A small target card on the right shows the mat to copy when a challenge gives one. The frame can show 10, 12 or 16 slits: the cards of a challenge set the number. Controls: drag cards into the rule line of a row in order, for example 2, over, 1, under, (repeat); a Weave button that colours the row from its cards; a Rows repeat from here button to tap on the row that is the same as Row 1; Undo, Hint, Retry (clears the row being built), Reset (clears the frame), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: a row list on the left that gives every woven row in words, for example Row 3: 2 under, 1 over (repeat); a slit counter for the row being built (for example 10 of 10 slits); the number of rows woven; a marker under the row chosen as the repeat; and a card number out of 6.
feedback: A row built from cards is woven with a gentle slide and the row list adds its words, for example Row 1: 3 over, 2 under (repeat).
If the row does not fill the slits, a soft amber note says how many slits are left, for example: Your row covers 9 of 10 slits: one more step is needed.
A row that swaps over and under in the row above gets a soft green note: Row 3 swaps over and under in Row 1: 2 under, 1 over.

When a row is tapped as the repeat but is not the same as Row 1, the tool lays the two rows one over the other and shows the first slit where they differ, in soft amber. It says: Not the same as Row 1 yet. Move on to the next row.
When a row starts its pattern in the same place as the row above, the tool says: Each new row can begin at a different place in the pattern. Compare where the first group starts.
tool_config.done_when: The rows of every card are built from cards and woven, the repeat is found on the rows of practice values and on the four rules, and the student has written the steps of a design until it repeats.

challenges: Card 1 (practice values, 12 slits): build Row 1 from the cards: 1 over, 3 under (repeat). Press Weave. How many slits go over and how many go under? Answer: the row goes over, under, under, under, over, under, under, under, over, under, under, under, so 3 slits go over and 9 go under, and 3 + 9 = 12.

Card 2 (practice values, 12 slits): build Row 2 so that it swaps over and under in Row 1. Answer: Row 2: 1 under, 3 over (repeat), which goes under, over, over, over, under, over, over, over, under, over, over, over.

Card 3 (practice values, 12 slits): build Row 1: 2 over, 1 under (repeat). Then build Row 2 as Row 1 moved one slit to the right, so that the last step comes round to the front. Answer: Row 2: 1 under (do not repeat), 2 over, 1 under (repeat), which goes under, over, over, under, over, over, under, over, over, under, over, over.

Card 4 (practice values, 12 slits): build Row 3 and Row 4 in the same way, each one moved one slit to the right. Which row is the same as Row 1? Tap Rows repeat from here on it. Challenge: 'Try to weave a pattern, using the rules given below. Row 1: 2 over, 1 under, 2 over, 1 under, ... (repeat). Row 2: 1 under (do not repeat), 3 over, 3 under, 3 over, 3 under, ... (repeat). media.teaching_notes: Predict first: a strip goes over, over, over, under, under, and then does the same again. How can you tell a friend this row in a few words, without saying every slit? Count the steps that stay together: 3 over, then 2 under. Over means the strip lies on top and shows. Under means it goes below. That group comes again and again, so we say repeat. The row is: 3 over, 2 under (repeat). The next row swaps over and under. Where Row 1 goes over, Row 2 goes under. So Row 2 is: 3 under, 2 over (repeat). Your maths book weaves a paper mat this way. The slits are cut in a paper 30 cm long, with a gap of 3 cm at the top and the bottom, so the slits are 30 − 3 − 3 = 24 cm long. Eight strips that are 3 cm wide fill them: 8 × 3 = 24 cm. Rule: describe a row by counting the over and under steps, then say repeat. 1. Read the strip slit by slit: over, over, over, under, under, over, over, over, under, under. Over means the strip lies on top and shows. 2. Count the steps that stay together: 3 over, then 2 under. 3. The same group comes again, so the row repeats: Row 1: 3 over, 2 under (repeat). 4. Row 2 swaps over and under: every over becomes under and every under becomes over. 5. So Row 2 goes under, under, under, over, over, under, under, under, over, over: Row 2: 3 under, 2 over (repeat). 6. Check: each group has 3 + 2 = 5 slits, and two groups make 5 + 5 = 10 slits, the whole row. Answer: Row 1: 3 over, 2 under (repeat). Row 2: 3 under, 2 over (repeat)

Let us make paper mats. You will need: A coloured paper (30 cm long and 20 cm wide) and eight paper strips of two different colours (3 cm wide and longer than 20 cm).
Fold the coloured paper in half along the longer side.
Draw vertical lines at equal distances from the closed end and cut slits leaving a gap of 3 cm at the top.
Carefully unfold the paper. There will be no cuts in the paper at the top and the bottom.
Take one colour strip and weave it across the slits going 1 under and 1 over, and again 1 under and 1 over. Repeat it for the first row.
Take one more strip of another colour and weave it across the slits going 1 over and 1 under, and again 1 over and 1 under. Repeat it for the second row.
Weave all the strips in the same alternating pattern. Neatly fold any extra strip ends behind the mat. Your mat is ready!
We can describe the pattern of the above weave as follows. Row 1: 1 under, 1 over, 1 under, 1 over, ... (repeat). Row 2: 1 over, 1 under, 1 over, 1 under, ... (repeat).

content.text:
1. Predict first: a strip goes over, over, over, under, under, and then does the same again. How can you tell a friend this row in a few words, without saying every slit?
2. Count the steps that stay together: 3 over, then 2 under. Over means the strip lies on top and shows. Under means it goes below.
3. That group comes again and again, so we say repeat. The row is: 3 over, 2 under (repeat).
4. The next row swaps over and under. Where Row 1 goes over, Row 2 goes under. So Row 2 is: 3 under, 2 over (repeat).
5. Your maths book weaves a paper mat this way. The slits are cut in a paper 30 cm long, with a gap of 3 cm at the top and the bottom, so the slits are 30 − 3 − 3 = 24 cm long. Eight strips that are 3 cm wide fill them: 8 × 3 = 24 cm.
6. Rule: describe a row by counting the over and under steps, then say repeat.

content.text:
Worked example: A mat has 10 slits. A strip goes over, over, over, under, under, over, over, over, under, under. Describe Row 1 in words. Then describe Row 2, where every strip swaps over and under.
1. Read the strip slit by slit: over, over, over, under, under, over, over, over, under, under. Over means the strip lies on top and shows.
2. Count the steps that stay together: 3 over, then 2 under.
3. The same group comes again, so the row repeats: Row 1: 3 over, 2 under (repeat).
4. Row 2 swaps over and under: every over becomes under and every under becomes over.
5. So Row 2 goes under, under, under, over, over, under, under, under, over, over: Row 2: 3 under, 2 over (repeat).
6. Check: each group has 3 + 2 = 5 slits, and two groups make 5 + 5 = 10 slits, the whole row.
Answer: Row 1: 3 over, 2 under (repeat). Row 2: 3 under, 2 over (repeat)

media.teaching_notes: 1. Over means the strip lies on top and shows. Under means it goes below. 2. Row 1: 2 over, 1 under, 2 over, 1 under, ... (repeat). The strip goes over, over, under again and again. 3. Row 2: say 1 under once (do not repeat), then 3 over, 3 under, 3 over, 3 under, ... (repeat). 4. Row 3: 2 under, 1 over, 2 under, ... (repeat). This swaps over and under in Row 1. 5. Row 4: say 1 over once (do not repeat), then 3 under, 3 over, ... (repeat). This swaps over and under in Row 2. 6. Row 5 follows the first rule again, so it is the same as Row 1. The pattern repeats after 4 rows. 7. Check: 4 rows repeated 4 times make 4 × 4 = 16 rows, the whole mat. Answer: Sample answer: Row 1: 2 over, 1 under; Row 2: 1 under, then 3 over, 3 under; Row 3 swaps Row 1; Row 4 swaps Row 2. Row 5 is Row 1: it repeats after 4 rows. Your answer may differ.

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M1.S3.T3.C7.IMG1}}
1. The mat has $8$ slits, and each row is one strip. Over means the strip shows on top.
2. Row $1$: $2$ over, $1$ under, $2$ over, $1$ under, ... goes over, over, under, over, over, under, over, over across the $8$ slits.
3. Row $2$: $2$ under, $1$ over, $2$ under, $1$ over, ... goes under, under, over, under, under, over, under, under.
[Image: Weaving Mats: Ans1: solution]
4. Row $2$ swaps over and under in Row $1$: where Row $1$ goes over, Row $2$ goes under.
5. Go on in the same way: Rows $3$, $5$ and $7$ are like Row $1$, and Rows $4$, $6$ and $8$ are like Row $2$.
6. Weave the $8$ strips one by one, with one colour for all rows or two colours.
7. Check: Row $1$ uses $2 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 2 = 8$ slits, and so does Row $2$.
Answer: Sample answer: Row $1$ goes over, over, under (repeat) and Row $2$ swaps it: under, under, over (repeat). Odd rows are like Row $1$, even rows like Row $2$. Your answer may differ.
[Image: Weaving Mats: Ans1: solution (continued)]

media.title: Fit Around a Point
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Fit Around a Point
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M2.S5.T5.C16.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity (fit shapes round a point and watch the gap and the overlap)
- Textbook source: Shapes and Patterns, Tiling and Tessellation: three pentagons round a point, the Find Out questions on triangles, squares, five squares and hexagons, and the regular octagon (developer only). Practice values: a hexagon with triangles, a square with triangles, and a hexagon with 2 squares and 1 triangle.
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student sees that shapes fit round a point only when their corners fill the space with no gap and no overlap, and finds how many of a regular shape fit.
- Out of scope: measuring any angle, giving corner sizes in numbers, shapes that are not regular, and drawing patterns (next tool).
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- A tile-shop table seen from above: a round cream felt mat on dark wood with a shiny brass pin in the middle (the point). The mat is the largest thing on the stage. A shelf along the bottom edge holds five glossy ceramic tiles (photo cut-outs, all sides the same length): an equilateral triangle, a square, a regular pentagon, a regular hexagon and a regular octagon.
- Around the pin a faint ring, like a clock face with no numbers, fills with colour as tiles are placed.
- Instruction line: "Put one corner of a tile on the brass pin."
- The square tile on the shelf pulses once.
2. Scene and Objects
- Mat and pin: the pin is a small brass dome. Each tile has a side about one ninth of the stage height; a tile on the shelf is half size.
- Space ring: each tile with a corner on the pin colours its own wedge of the ring in its tile colour (triangle teal, square red, pentagon yellow, hexagon blue, octagon purple). Empty ring stays pale, overlapped ring flashes orange, a full ring glows green.
- Status line under the mat: "No gap, no overlap", "A gap is left" or "Overlap", with a note on whether the gap is big enough for one more of the tile in hand ("The gap is too small for another pentagon"). Counter: "tiles at the pin: 3".
- Goal chip on the mat, for example "No gap". Bottom buttons (large, three only): Hint, Reset, Next. Next is locked until the goal chip is green.
3. Main Interaction
- Drag a tile to the mat. Near the pin it snaps with one corner on the pin; the first tile can be turned with a small round handle. Each next tile snaps edge to edge to the open side of the tile before it, going round the pin, and may be placed even if it would overlap (the overlap flashes orange). A tile dropped far from the pin slides back to the shelf.
- Tap the last tile placed to lift it off. Reset clears the mat. At most 8 tiles can be at the pin.
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Two hexagons are at the pin. Fill the gap with triangles." Goal chip: "No gap". Setup: 2 hexagons edge to edge at the pin; six tick marks on the ring, each one triangle corner wide. Help: guided (tick marks). Guess: "How many triangles will fill the gap?" with cards 1, 2 and 3. Result: after 2 triangles the ring closes and glows green. Why line: "A hexagon corner takes the space of 2 triangle corners. 2 hexagons take 4, and 2 triangles add 2 more: 4 + 2 = 6, and 6 triangle corners fill the space."
- Activity 2 (guided less). Goal line: "Put a square at the pin and fit triangles next to it. Can the space be filled?" Goal chip: "Square and triangles". Setup: 1 square, no tick marks. Guess: "Will the square and triangles fill the space exactly?" with cards "Yes", "No, a gap is left" and "No, they overlap". Result: 4 triangles fit and a gap is left that is smaller than one triangle corner; a fifth triangle overlaps. The chip is green once 4 triangles are placed and a fifth is tried. Why line: "The gap is too small for another triangle, and a fifth triangle would overlap. A gap that is too small does not count as fitting." Help: guided less, no tick marks.
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "Use a hexagon, 2 squares and 1 triangle to fill the space round the pin." Goal chip: "Fill the space". Setup: 1 hexagon at the pin. Guess: "After the hexagon and the 2 squares, how much room is left?" with cards "A gap too small for a triangle", "Room for exactly 1 triangle" and "No room: they overlap". Result: any order round the pin works; the ring closes. Why line: "1 hexagon, 2 squares and 1 triangle: their 4 corners fill the space round the pin with no gap and no overlap." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1. Goal line: "We have placed 3 pentagons around a point. Can we fit one more into the empty space?" Goal chip: "Fourth pentagon". Setup: 3 pentagons at the pin, a gap left. Guess: cards "Yes" and "No". The child drags a fourth pentagon: it lies over the others. Result: No. Why line: "The gap is smaller than one pentagon corner, so a fourth pentagon would overlap. Regular pentagons do not tessellate." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 2. Goal line: "Can regular triangles fit together at a point without any gap? How many of them fit together?" Goal chip: "Triangles". Setup: empty mat. Guess: number cards 4, 5, 6 and 7. Result: the ring closes after 6 triangles. Why line: "6 triangles fit with no gap and no overlap. With 5 a gap is left, and a 7th would overlap." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 3. Goal line: "Can squares (a regular 4-sided shape) fit together around a point without any gap or overlap? Try it out using cutouts of squares. How many squares did you need?" Goal chip: "Squares". Guess: number cards 3, 4 and 5. Result: the ring closes after 4 squares. Why line: "4 squares fit: their 4 right angle corners fill the space. With 3 a gap is left." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 4. Goal line: "Can five squares fit together around a point without any gaps or overlaps? Why or why not?" Goal chip: "Five squares". Guess: cards "Yes" and "No". The child tries 5 squares; then 3 "why" cards appear: "4 squares already fill the space, so a fifth overlaps", "A gap is left" and "Squares are too big". Result: No; the first why card is right. Why line: "4 squares already fill the space round the point, so a fifth square would overlap the first." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 5. Goal line: "Can regular hexagons (6-sided shapes with equal sides) fit together around a point without any gaps or overlaps? Try and see. How many fit together at a point?" Goal chip: "Hexagons". Guess: number cards 2, 3 and 4. Result: the ring closes after 3 hexagons. Why line: "3 hexagons fit with no gap and no overlap. With 2 a gap is left, and a 4th would overlap." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 6. Goal line: "Do regular octagons fit together without any gaps or overlaps? Try drawing the same and check." Goal chip: "Octagons". Guess: cards "Yes" and "No". The child places octagons: 2 fit and a third lies over them. Result: No. A bonus card then says "Try a square in the gap" and a square fits exactly. Why line: "2 octagons leave a gap that is too small for a third octagon, so regular octagons do not tessellate. A square fits that gap: 2 octagons and 1 square fill the point." Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- Placing tiles one by one, the child sees the ring fill up. A regular shape fits when whole corners of that tile fill the ring exactly: 6 triangles, 4 squares, 3 hexagons. If the corners leave a gap smaller than another corner, or one more tile overlaps, it does not fit and does not tessellate.
- Rules in the child's words: "Shapes fit round a point when their corners fill the space with no gap and no overlap." "A gap that is too small for another shape does not count."
6. Feedback and Hints
- Wrong answer: red strip, a small shake of the object, and one friendly line naming the mistake and what to look at. No scores; trying again is always free. Correct: the ring glows green, the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce, the pill gets a tick and Next unlocks.
- Tile dropped away from the pin -> "Put one corner of the tile on the brass pin." The pin pulses.
- Says pentagons or octagons fit -> "Not every regular shape fits round a point. Look at the gap that is left." The gap in the ring glows.
- Says a small gap is fine -> "A small gap is still a gap, so this shape does not tessellate by itself." The gap glows.
- Counts tiles that do not touch the pin -> "Count only the tiles that have a corner on the pin." The corners at the pin pulse.
- Says 5 squares fit -> "The first 4 squares already fill the space. Where would the fifth go?" The ring pulses.
- Hint button, 3 levels. (1) Words: "Which tile are you fitting, and is one corner on the pin?" (2) Visual clue: the gap in the ring glows and the note says if one more tile is too big or too small for it. (3) Almost the answer: the tool places the first two tiles edge to edge round the pin.
- Edge cases: 5 triangles leave a gap big enough for exactly one more triangle; 3 pentagons leave a gap smaller than a pentagon corner; 2 octagons leave a gap exactly the size of one square corner.
7. Ending
- A star challenge is done when its result in section 4 is reached; the end screen follows when all chips are green.
- End screen: confetti once. "Well done!" Remember: "Shapes fit round a point when their corners fill the space with no gap and no overlap." "6 triangles, 4 squares and 3 hexagons fit round a point." "Regular pentagons and octagons leave a gap that is too small, so they do not tessellate." Think and talk: "A square and 2 hexagons are at a point. Is there room for anything else?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Images: dark wood table top view (photo); round cream felt mat; brass pin (photo cut-out); five glossy ceramic tiles (photo-style, all with the same side). Ring, tick marks and cards are code-drawn. No people. English only.

tool_config.idea: Fit regular triangles, squares, pentagons, hexagons and octagons around a point and count how many fit, watching for the gap and the overlap: some shapes fill the space exactly, and others leave a gap that is too small to use.
tool_config.title: Fit Around a Point
tool_config.screen: A tile mat on the craft table, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. A cream mat with one orange point marked in the middle is the largest thing on screen, and the shapes are placed on it. On a shelf at the left sit cutouts of five shapes, each with every side the same length: an equilateral triangle, a square, a regular pentagon, a regular hexagon and a regular octagon. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: drag a shape so that one corner sits on the marked point; the shape turns and snaps edge to edge to the shape before it; Undo; Hint; Retry (clears the mat); Reset (clears the mat and the counter); Back and Next in the same places on every card. A gap that is left glows soft amber, and a shape that lies over another shows its overlap glowing soft amber. Read-outs: a counter shapes at the point (for example 3), a status line that says gap left, no gap, or overlap, a note that tells whether the gap left is big enough for one more of the shape in hand, and a card number out of 7.
feedback: When the corners fill the space, the glow turns soft green and the status line says: No gap, no overlap. 6 triangles fit.
When the space is not full, the gap glows soft amber and the note says how it compares with one more shape, for example: The gap is too small for another pentagon.
When a shape would lie over another, the part that overlaps glows soft amber and the note says: A fifth square would overlap the first: 4 squares fill the space.
A shape dropped far from the point slides back with a clue: Put one corner of the shape on the marked point.
A small gap is never accepted as fitting: the tool says: A gap is left, so this shape does not tessellate by itself. It never shows a red cross.
tool_config.done_when: Triangles, squares, hexagons, pentagons and octagons have each been fitted round the point and counted, the gap that is too small has been seen for pentagons and octagons, and the two questions of your maths book are answered.

Card 3: fit regular hexagons round the point. How many fit? Answer: 3 hexagons fit, with no gap and no overlap.

Card 4: fit regular pentagons round the point. How many fit, and can one more go in the gap? Answer: 3 pentagons fit and a gap is left. The gap is too small for a 4th pentagon, which would overlap, so regular pentagons do not tessellate.

topics.summary: Shapes that have equal sides are called regular shapes. Shapes fit around a point when their corners fill the space with no gap and no overlap, and then they tessellate.

content.text:
We often use tiles of the same shape or a combination of shapes to cover a region.
You can see pentagons (5-sided figures) in this figure. As all its sides are equal it is a regular pentagon.
Shapes that have equal sides are called regular shapes.
A regular octagon means a shape with eight equal sides.
Regular octagons do not tessellate.

Pentagons cannot fill a region without leaving gaps. So, we say that regular pentagons do not tessellate.
Regular triangles when fitted around a point leave no gaps and there is no overlap.
Triangles with all equal sides are also called equilateral triangles. Therefore, equilateral triangles tessellate.

Answer: No. $2$ octagons side by side leave a gap that is too small for a third, so regular octagons do not tessellate. A square fits that gap.

{{DIAGRAM:M2.S7.T7.C24.IMG1}}
1. Put one square with a corner on the point. A corner of a square is a right angle.
2. Put the next square beside it, edge to edge, with its corner on the point too.
3. After $4$ squares the last one touches the first one. The $4$ corners fill the space.
4. Check: $3$ squares leave a gap and a $5\text{th}$ square would overlap, so exactly $4$ are needed.
Answer: Yes. $4$ squares fit around a point with no gap and no overlap, because $4$ right angle corners fill the space.

content.text: Can five squares fit together around a point without any gaps or overlaps? Why or why not?
content.question: Can five squares fit together around a point without any gaps or overlaps? Why or why not?
content.book_number: Find Out: five squares
content.question_tex: Can five squares fit together around a point without any gaps or overlaps? Why or why not?
content.publication_text: Can five squares fit together around a point without any gaps or overlaps? Why or why not?

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M2.S7.T7.C26.IMG1}}
1. Fit squares round the point one by one. After $4$ squares the space is full.
2. A fifth square has no room. It would sit on top of the first square: an overlap.
3. So five squares cannot fit around a point without an overlap.
4. Check: $4$ squares fit exactly, and $5$ is one more than $4$, so there is no room for it.
Answer: No. $4$ squares already fill the space round the point, so a fifth square would overlap the first one.

media.title: Pattern Tiler
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Pattern Tiler
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M2.S8.T8.C30.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity (continue patterns of two shapes and list the shapes that meet at a point)
- Textbook source: Shapes and Patterns, Tessellation Patterns: the hexagon and triangle pattern, the octagon and square pattern, the squares and triangles pattern with five marked points, and "Create similar patterns" (developer only). Practice values: a border of squares and hexagons.
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student lists the shapes that meet at a point of a pattern made with two shapes, tells whether the same set meets at every point, and continues the pattern.
- Out of scope: measuring angles, naming other patterns, shapes that are not on the shelf.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- A tiler's pegboard (photo-style): a light wooden board with a grid of small grey pegs (dots). A straight border strip of 4 glossy ceramic tiles lies in the middle, the largest thing on the stage: square, hexagon, square, hexagon, edge to edge (the hexagon has a vertical side left and right). A shelf under the board holds the tiles.
- Instruction line: "Add 4 more tiles to make a border of 8 tiles. The tiles take turns."
- The shelf's square tile pulses once.
2. Scene and Objects
- Boards (the stage changes with the activity): the border board, a triangle dot grid, and two square dot grids (one for octagons and squares, one for tilted squares and triangles).
- Tiles (ceramic cut-outs, all with the same side): regular hexagon, square, equilateral triangle, regular octagon; and for the last pattern a tilted square (its sides go 1 across and 2 up on the dot grid) and a triangle with a base of 2 dot steps and two longer equal sides. New tiles start plain white when a card asks for colouring.
- Marked points: red pins, each with a small ring that fills with the colours of the tile corners at it: full means no gap and no overlap, part-empty means a gap, overlap flashes orange.
- Five paint pots (purple, yellow, green, blue, orange) along the bottom edge. Checker card: opens at a tapped point and lists its shapes, for example "2 octagons, 1 square".
- Goal chip, for example "8 tiles". Bottom buttons (large, three only): Hint, Reset, Next. Next is locked until the goal chip is green.
3. Main Interaction
- Drag a tile from the shelf; it snaps to the dots and edge to edge to its neighbour. Small round handles turn and flip a tile in hand. Drag a placed tile back to the shelf to remove it.
- Tap a point (a corner shared by tiles, or a pin): the checker card lists the shapes there. Tap a second point: the card adds "Same set" or "Different sets".
- Tap a paint pot, then tap tiles to colour them. Reset clears the last tiles placed.
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Add 4 more tiles to make a border of 8 tiles. The tiles take turns." Goal chip: "8 tiles". Setup: square, hexagon, square, hexagon. Help: guided, each join shows a tag with the two shapes that meet. Guess: "How many squares will the border of 8 tiles have?" with cards 3, 4 and 5. Result: the tiles go square, hexagon, square, hexagon, square, hexagon, square, hexagon. Why line: "The tiles take turns, so 4 squares and 4 hexagons make 4 + 4 = 8 tiles."
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Tap two joins and read the lists. Do the same shapes meet?" Goal chip: "Compare joins". Setup: the border of 8 tiles. Guess: "The lists will be:" cards "The same" and "Different". Result: the card says "Same set: 1 square, 1 hexagon at both joins". Why line: "A square is always next to a hexagon, so the same two shapes meet at every join." Help: guided.
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "A new border does not take turns. Tap three joins and compare." Goal chip: "Compare 3 joins". Setup: a border of 6 tiles: square, hexagon, hexagon, square, hexagon, hexagon. Guess: "The same shapes meet at every join:" cards "Yes" and "No". Result: one join has a square and a hexagon, the next has 2 hexagons, the next a hexagon and a square; the card says "Different sets". Why line: "One join has 2 hexagons, so the same set does not meet everywhere. The shapes do not take turns." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1. Goal line: "Here is a tessellating pattern with more than one shape. What shapes have been used in this pattern? ___, ___." Goal chip: "Name the shapes". Setup: a patch of the hexagon and triangle pattern. Guess: the child taps two shape cards out of "Regular hexagon", "Equilateral triangle", "Square", "Regular pentagon" and "Regular octagon"; the tiles of the chosen shapes glow. Result: regular hexagons and equilateral triangles. Why line: "At every meeting point 2 hexagons and 2 triangles come together, in the order hexagon, triangle, hexagon, triangle." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 2. Goal line: "Continue the pattern given below and colour it appropriately." Goal chip: "Continue". Setup: 3 purple hexagons that touch at corners and the 13 yellow triangles round them. Guess: "The next hexagon will touch the others at:" cards "a corner" and "a side". The child places 2 more hexagons and the 6 triangles they need, then colours the new tiles. Done when each shape has one colour. Result: 5 hexagons and 19 triangles. Why line: "The hexagons touch only at corners, and a triangle sits on each side of a hexagon." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 3. Goal line: "Look at the pattern given below. What shapes are coming together at the marked points? Are the same set of shapes coming together at these points? Continue the pattern and colour it appropriately." Goal chip: "Marked points". Setup: 4 rows of 4 green octagons with 9 small blue squares between them, and 4 red pins on the corners of one small square. Guess: "The same set of shapes meets at all 4 points:" cards "Yes" and "No". The child taps each pin, then adds a fifth column on the right (4 octagons and 3 small squares) and colours the new tiles green and blue. Result: at each pin 2 octagons and 1 square meet. Why line: "2 octagons and 1 square fill the space round a point, and the same set meets at every pin." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 4. Goal line: "Here is a tiling pattern made using two different shapes, squares and triangles. Are the triangles equilateral? Why or why not?" Goal chip: "Equilateral?". Setup: 3 tilted squares and 2 triangles joined as in the pattern, and a paper strip as long as a square's side. Guess: cards "Yes" and "No". The child lays the strip along each side of a triangle. Result: 2 sides are as long as the strip and the third side is shorter (it counts exactly 2 dot steps). Why line: "Two sides of each triangle are as long as a side of a square and the third side is shorter, so the triangles are not equilateral." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 5. Goal line: "What shapes are coming together at the marked points? Are the same set of shapes coming together at these points? Continue the pattern and colour it appropriately." Goal chip: "5 full points". Setup: the same 3 tilted squares and 2 triangles with 5 red pins. Guess: "How many shapes will meet at each pin?" cards 4, 5 and 6. The child places tiles round every pin until its ring is full (the simplest way uses 10 tiles: 3 squares and 7 triangles), reads the lists, and colours squares purple and triangles orange. Result: 2 squares and 3 triangles at every pin. Why line: "2 squares and 3 triangles fill the space round a point, and the same set meets at all 5 pins: 2 + 3 = 5 shapes." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 6. Goal line: "Create similar patterns using other cutouts of shapes." Goal chip: "My pattern". Setup: an empty dot grid and all the tiles on the shelf. Guess: "Pick 2 shapes you think fit together round a point:" cards "Square and triangle", "Pentagon and square" and "Hexagon and octagon". The child builds a patch of at least 8 tiles of 2 shapes with at least one full point, then taps two points to compare. Result: the card lists what meets at each point. Any 2 shapes that fill a point with no gap and no overlap are accepted. Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- A pattern of two shapes repeats the shapes in the same order, so the same shapes meet at the points; when the order changes (2 hexagons in a row), the shapes at a join change.
- Rules in the child's words: "At each meeting point, list the shapes that come together." "If the same set meets at every point, the pattern can go on in the same way."
6. Feedback and Hints
- Wrong answer: red strip, a small shake of the object, and one friendly line naming the mistake and what to look at. No scores; trying again is always free. Correct: the tiles glow green once, the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce, the pill gets a tick and Next unlocks.
- Tile in the wrong place -> "Put the square where four octagons meet." The right place pulses.
- Says the sets are the same when they are not (Activity 3) -> "Different sets. Look again at the shapes that meet at each point." The two joins glow.
- Leaves a gap at a pin -> "A gap is left here. Which shape would fill it?" The gap glows orange; a small gap is never accepted.
- Says the triangle is equilateral -> "Lay the strip along all three sides. Do they match?" The third side pulses.
- Mixes colours of one shape -> "Colour all the hexagons the same, and all the triangles the same." The odd tile pulses.
- Hint button, 3 levels. (1) Words: "Which point are you looking at? Name every shape that has a corner there." (2) Visual clue: the corners at the point glow. (3) Almost the answer: the tool shows the list at the first point.
- Edge cases: a point that is not full lists "a gap".
7. Ending
- A star challenge is done when its result in section 4 is reached; the end screen follows when all chips are green.
- End screen: confetti once. "Well done!" Remember: "At each meeting point, list the shapes that come together." "If the same set of shapes meets at every point, the pattern goes on in the same way." Think and talk: "A border goes square, hexagon, hexagon, square, hexagon, hexagon. What would you change so that the same shapes meet at every join?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Images: light wooden pegboard; glossy ceramic tiles in the shapes above; paper strip; red pins (photo cut-outs); paint pots (flat). Dot grids and cards are code-drawn. No people. English only.

tool_config.idea: Continue a pattern made of two shapes and list the shapes that meet at a point. Placing the tiles is the pattern, and the meeting-point list makes the question whether the same set of shapes meets at every point something that can be seen.
tool_config.title: Pattern Tiler
tool_config.screen: A floor of dots on the craft table, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. A board with a dot grid is the largest thing on screen: a triangle dot grid for hexagons and triangles, and a square dot grid for squares, octagons and tilted squares. On a shelf at the left sit cutouts of a regular hexagon, an equilateral triangle, a regular octagon, a square, and the tilted square and the triangle with two equal sides that your maths book uses in its last pattern. Four or five marked points sit on the board when a card asks about them. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: drag a tile, turn it with the Turn button, and it snaps to the dots and to the tile next to it; tap a marked point to open the checker list; a colour tool with purple, yellow, green, blue and orange; Undo; Hint; Retry (clears the last tiles placed); Reset (clears the board); Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the checker list for a tapped point, written as a count for each shape, for example 2 octagons, 1 square; a line that says same set or different set when two points are compared; and a card number out of 6.
feedback: A tile that snaps to the dots and to its neighbour slides into place with a soft click, and the checker list for its corners updates.
Tapping a point opens the checker list and says what meets there, for example: At this point 2 octagons and 1 square meet.
When two points are compared the tool says either: Same set, 2 octagons and 1 square at both points, or: Different sets. Look again at the shapes that meet at each point.
A point where the tiles leave a gap glows soft amber with the note: A gap is left here. Which shape would fill it? A small gap is not accepted as fitting.
A tile put in the wrong place slides back with a clue, for example: Put the square where four octagons meet. The tool never shows a red cross.
tool_config.done_when: The border is continued, hexagons and triangles are placed round a point, two points are compared, the border that does not take turns has been checked, and the two questions of your maths book are answered.

challenges: Card 1 (practice values): a border starts with 4 tiles: square, triangle, square, triangle. Place 4 more tiles to make a border of 8 tiles. How many squares and how many triangles are there? Answer: the tiles go square, triangle, square, triangle, square, triangle, square, triangle: 4 squares and 4 triangles, and 4 + 4 = 8.

Card 2: on the triangle dot grid, place hexagons and triangles round one point until the space is full. Answer: 2 hexagons and 2 triangles fill the point with no gap and no overlap, in the order hexagon, triangle, hexagon, triangle.

Card 3: tap two points of your pattern and read the checker lists. Are the same shapes meeting at both? Answer: at both points 2 hexagons and 2 triangles meet, so the same set of shapes meets at both points.

Card 4 (practice values): the tool shows a border that goes square, triangle, triangle, square, triangle, triangle, and so on. Tap three joins and compare the lists. Answer: one join has a square and a triangle, the next has two triangles, and the next has a triangle and a square, so the same set does not meet at every join, because the shapes do not take turns.

Challenge: 'Look at the pattern given below. What shapes are coming together at the marked points? Are the same set of shapes coming together at these points? Continue the pattern and colour it appropriately.' The board shows 4 rows of 4 regular octagons with a small square between each group of four. Answer: 2 octagons and 1 square come together at each marked point, and yes, it is the same set every time. Continue with octagons edge to edge and a small square wherever four octagons meet. Your colours may differ.

Challenge: 'Here is a tessellating pattern with more than one shape. What shapes have been used in this pattern?' The board shows a pattern of hexagons and small triangles. Answer: regular hexagons and equilateral triangles.

The tool shows the list at the first point: 2 octagons and 1 square. Now tap the next point and compare the lists yourself.

content.text:
Worked example: A border has 12 tiles in a row. The tiles go square, triangle, square, triangle, and so on. How many squares and how many triangles are there, and which shapes meet at every join?
1. The tiles take turns: square, triangle, square, triangle, ... The first tile is a square.
2. Every second tile is a square, so there are 12 ÷ 2 = 6 squares.
3. The other tiles are triangles: 12 − 6 = 6 triangles.
4. Check the count: 6 + 6 = 12 tiles.
5. Look at each join between two neighbours. Every join has a square on one side and a triangle on the other.
6. So the same two kinds of shape meet at every join: a square and a triangle.
7. Check: the tiles never put two squares or two triangles side by side, because they take turns.
Answer: 6 squares and 6 triangles, because 6 + 6 = 12. At every join a square and a triangle meet, the same set each time

At every corner inside the frame 2 hexagons and 2 triangles meet in the order hexagon, triangle, hexagon, triangle. The exact clipped outline of every piece is listed in content.polygons. 1. Look at the shapes that repeat in the pattern.

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M2.S9.T9.C38.IMG1}}
1. An equilateral triangle has all $3$ sides equal. Compare the sides of one triangle by counting along the dots.
2. Two sides of the triangle are as long as a side of a square, a little more than $2$ grid steps.
3. The third side is shorter. It is exactly $2$ grid steps.
4. So two sides are equal and the third side is not.
5. Check: for an equilateral triangle all $3$ sides must be equal, and here the third side is shorter.
Answer: No. Two sides of each triangle are as long as a side of a square, and the third side is shorter, so the triangles are not equilateral.
