content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M3.S17.T17.C90.IMG1}}
1. Use some or all of the $7$ pieces. The pieces must not overlap, and they must fill the outline with no gap.
2. Rectangle: put the medium triangle in the middle with its longest side at the bottom. Put a small triangle in the gap on each side. The $3$ pieces fill the rectangle.
[Image: Tangram: Ans5: solution]
3. Slanted parallelogram: put the medium triangle on the left. Put the $2$ small triangles together on the right, so that they make a second triangle the size of the medium one. The $2$ triangles side by side make the slanted shape.
4. Triangle: the medium triangle fills it, with its longest side at the bottom. The $2$ small triangles also fill it, side by side with their right angles together at the middle of the bottom.
5. Four-sided shape with a short top and a long bottom: put the parallelogram on the left and the medium triangle on the right, with the longest side of the medium triangle at the bottom.
6. More than one way: the rectangle can also be made from the square and the $2$ small triangles, and the parallelogram from the square with a small triangle on each side.
7. Check: each outline is filled with no gap and no overlap.
Answer: Sample answer: rectangle and parallelogram: medium triangle and $2$ small triangles. Triangle: medium triangle. Last shape: parallelogram and medium triangle. Your answer may differ.
[Image: Tangram: Ans5: solution (continued)]

media.title: Shape Detective
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Shape Detective
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M3.S18.T18.C92.2D1
- Tool type: Puzzle (make four-sided shapes with two locks, then match statements to shapes)
- Textbook source: Shapes and Patterns, Which Shape Am I?: the table of seven statements and the shapes Square, Rectangle, Rhombus and Parallelogram (developer only). Practice values: a first rectangle 10 cm by 3 cm, the statements "All my sides are equal" and "I have 4 right angles".
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student tells a square, a rectangle, a rhombus and a parallelogram apart by checking the sides and then the angles, and sees that one statement can describe more than one shape.
- Out of scope: kites, measuring angles, and any shape with more than 4 sides.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- A detective's cork pinboard seen from above. In the middle, a red string is stretched round four brass pins and makes a rectangle (10 cm by 3 cm, with a small square mark at each right angle). It is the largest thing on the stage. Above the shape two brass dial locks sit side by side, "Sides" and "Angles", next to a brass name plate that reads "Rectangle". Four cards with outlines are pinned in a row along the bottom of the board: a green square, a purple rectangle, a blue rhombus (a slanted shape with equal sides) and a yellow parallelogram. Seven index cards numbered 1 to 7 lie on a shelf under the board.
- Instruction line: "Set both locks to make a square."
- The Sides lock pulses once.
2. Scene and Objects
- Shape: 4 round brass pins are the corners; the side lengths show next to each side in whole cm; a small square mark sits on every right angle.
- Sides lock, 3 positions: "Off", "Opposite sides equal" and "All sides equal". Angles lock, 2 positions: "Off" and "Right angles". The two locks decide what the other pins do when one pin is dragged.
- Name plate: "Four-sided shape", "Parallelogram", "Rhombus", "Rectangle" or "Square", always the most special name that fits.
- Index cards 1 to 7 carry the statements, in full, with the wording of the question. A small tester light sits on each card: green when it fits the shape on the board, orange with a reason when it does not.
- Shape cards: 4 pinned cards, each with a small tick box. A tally under each card counts the statements matched, for example "Rhombus: 3".
- Goal chip, for example "Make a square". Bottom buttons (large, three only): Hint, Reset, Next. Next is locked until the goal chip is green.
3. Main Interaction
- Drag a pin. With both locks Off the pins move one by one. With "Opposite sides equal" and Angles Off, the pin across from the dragged pin moves the other way, so the shape stays a parallelogram. With "All sides equal" and Angles Off, the other two pins turn too, so all 4 sides stay equal (a rhombus). With "Right angles" the shape stays a rectangle, or a square when "All sides equal" is also on.
- Turn a lock by tapping it. When a lock is changed, the shape rebuilds itself as the nearest shape of that kind (for example from a rectangle 10 by 3 to a square with sides of 10).
- Drag an index card onto the board to test it on the shape there, or onto a shape card to match it with that shape. A match is kept only if the statement is true for that shape; otherwise the card slides back with a clue.
- Reset clears the matches and unlocks both locks.
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Set both locks to make a square." Goal chip: "Make a square". Setup: the rectangle 10 by 3. Help: guided, each lock position shows a small label. Guess: "What will the name plate say?" with cards "Square", "Rectangle" and "Rhombus". Result: Sides lock "All sides equal" and Angles lock "Right angles"; the child drags a pin and the 4 sides grow and shrink together. Why line: "All 4 sides are equal and all 4 angles are right angles: a square."
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Now make a rectangle." Goal chip: "Make a rectangle". Help: guided. Guess: cards "Square", "Rectangle" and "Parallelogram" for the name plate with Sides lock "Opposite sides equal" and Angles lock "Right angles". Result: the child drags a pin; opposite sides stay equal and the 4 angles stay right angles, while sides next to each other can be different. Why line: "Opposite sides are equal and all 4 angles are right angles: a rectangle."
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "Make a shape with all sides equal and no right angle." Goal chip: "Make a rhombus". Setup: locks free. Guess: cards "Square", "Rhombus" and "Parallelogram". Result: Sides lock "All sides equal", Angles lock "Off"; the child drags a pin until no angle is a right angle (the shape is slanted). Why line: "All 4 sides are equal and the angles are not right angles: a rhombus." Help: independent.
- Activity 4 (independent). Goal line: "Make a shape with opposite sides equal, sides next to each other different, and no right angle." Goal chip: "Make a parallelogram". Guess: cards "Rectangle", "Rhombus" and "Parallelogram". Result: Sides lock "Opposite sides equal", Angles lock "Off"; the child drags a pin until two sides next to each other have different lengths and no angle is right. Why line: "Opposite sides are equal and the angles are not right angles: a parallelogram." Help: independent.
- Activity 5 (independent). Goal line: "Make each of your 4 shapes. Test the card 'All my sides are equal' on each one." Goal chip: "Test a card". Setup: a practice card "All my sides are equal" lies on the board. Guess: "On how many of the 4 shapes will it fit?" with cards 1, 2, 3 and 4. Result: it fits the square and the rhombus. Why line: "All sides equal is true for the square and the rhombus. In the rectangle and the parallelogram the sides next to each other can be different." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1. Goal line: "Match the statements with appropriate shapes. Do some of them describe more than one shape? (1) All my angles are right angles, but all my sides are not equal. (2) All my sides are equal, but all my angles are not. (3) My opposite angles are equal, but my sides do not make a right angle. (4) Two pairs of sides are equal, but they do not make a right angle. (5) All my sides make right angles with each other and are equal. (6) My opposite angles are equal and so are my sides. (7) My opposite angles are equal and my sides make right angles." Goal chip: "Match 7 statements". Guess: "How many of the 7 statements describe more than one shape?" with cards 2, 4 and 6. The child tests each statement on the board (using the locks) and matches it with every shape it fits. Truth table the tool uses: 1 Rectangle; 2 Rhombus; 3 Rhombus and Parallelogram; 4 Parallelogram and Rhombus; 5 Square; 6 Square, Rectangle, Rhombus and Parallelogram; 7 Square and Rectangle. The goal is done when all 13 matches are kept. Result: the tally reads Square: 3, Rectangle: 3, Rhombus: 4, Parallelogram: 3, and the line says "Statements 3, 4, 6 and 7 describe more than one shape." Why line: "A rhombus, a rectangle and a square all have opposite sides equal, so statement 6 fits all four shapes: 3 + 3 + 4 + 3 = 13 matches." Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- Dragging pins with the locks on, the child sees that two questions sort the four shapes: are all sides equal, and are all angles right angles. A shape can fit a statement and still be called by a more special name, so one statement can fit several shapes.
- Rules in the child's words: "Check the sides, then the angles." "All sides equal and right angles: square. Opposite sides equal and right angles: rectangle. All sides equal and no right angle: rhombus. Opposite sides equal and no right angle: parallelogram." "One statement can fit more than one shape."
6. Feedback and Hints
- Every wrong answer: the feedback strip turns red, the object shakes a little, and one friendly line names the mistake and what to look at. No scores; trying again is always free.
- Correct: the tester light and the matched card turn green, the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce, the pill gets a tick and Next unlocks.
- Matches statement 1 with the square -> "Statement 1 says the sides are not all equal, but a square has 4 equal sides." The 4 sides of the square pulse.
- Matches statement 2 with the square -> "Statement 2 says the angles are not all right angles, but a square has 4 right angles." The 4 right angle marks pulse.
- Matches statement 6 with only the parallelogram -> "A rectangle, a rhombus and a square also have opposite sides equal and opposite angles equal. Try them on the board." The other 3 shape cards pulse.

- Names a shape from the sides only -> "Check the sides first. Are all four equal? Then check the angles." The two locks pulse in turn.
- Hint button, 3 levels. (1) Words: "Read the statement slowly. What does it say about the sides, and what does it say about the angles?" (2) Visual clue: the board shows the shape for the statement and the tester light. (3) Almost the answer: "Statement 5 says all sides equal and all angles right angles: the name plate says Square", and the tool matches statement 5 with the square.

- A star challenge is done when its result in section 4 is reached; the end screen follows when all chips are green.

tool_config.idea: Drag the corners of one four-sided shape and switch two locks to see when it is a square, a rectangle, a rhombus or a parallelogram, then test seven statements about sides and angles and see that one statement can fit more than one shape.
tool_config.title: Shape Detective
tool_config.screen: The detective's board on the craft table, drawn as a warm 3-D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. A pinboard in the middle holds one four-sided shape on a dot grid, and it is the largest thing on screen. The shape has four round corner handles that can be dragged. Its four sides show their lengths in centimetres next to them (practice values), and every corner that is a right angle carries a small square mark. To the left of the board are two locks: a Sides lock with three positions, Off, Opposite sides equal and All sides equal, and an Angles lock with two positions, Off and Right angles. A name plate above the shape reads Four-sided shape, Parallelogram, Rhombus, Rectangle or Square, whichever fits the shape now. Along the bottom lies a shelf of seven statement cards numbered 1 to 7 with the book's wording, and on the right are four shape cards: Square, Rectangle, Rhombus and Parallelogram. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: drag a corner handle (the locks decide what the other corners do, so the sides or angles stay as set); switch each lock; drag a statement card onto the shape to test it, or onto a shape card to match it; Check, Hint, Undo, Retry (clears the last match), Reset (clears all matches and unlocks the shape), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the four side lengths, the right angle marks, the name plate, a tester light on each statement card that shows fits in green or look again in soft amber with the reason, and a match tally that counts how many statements are matched to each shape (for example Rhombus: 3).
feedback: A statement card dropped on a shape shows a green tester light when it fits and a soft amber light when it does not, with the reason, for example: Statement 7 fits the rectangle: its opposite angles are equal and its sides make right angles.
When a lock is set the shape keeps what the lock says while you drag. Under Opposite sides equal the other corners follow, so the opposite sides stay equal, and the name plate changes at once.
A rectangle also has opposite angles equal: statement 7 fits it too, so the tool says that one statement can fit more than one shape.
Statement 1 dropped on the square shows soft amber: all my angles are right angles is true for the square, but its sides are all equal, so all my sides are not equal does not fit.

A wrong match slides back with a clue such as: Check the sides first. Are all four equal? It never shows a red mark. A shape card that has a match gets a small green tick and the tally counts it, for example: Statement 3 fits 2 shapes.
tool_config.done_when: All four shapes have been made with the locks, statements have been tested on them, all seven statements are matched, and the student has said which statements fit more than one shape.

Card 2: set the Sides lock to Opposite sides equal and the Angles lock to Right angles, then drag a corner. Which shape is it? Answer: a rectangle. Opposite sides stay equal, the four angles stay right angles, and the sides next to each other can be different.

content.text: Match the statements with appropriate shapes. Do some of them describe more than one shape? $(1)$: All my angles are right angles, but all my sides are not equal. $(2)$: All my sides are equal, but all my angles are not. $(3)$: My opposite angles are equal, but my sides do not make a right angle. $(4)$: Two pairs of sides are equal, but they do not make a right angle. $(5)$: All my sides make right angles with each other and are equal. $(6)$: My opposite angles are equal and so are my sides. $(7)$: My opposite angles are equal and my sides make right angles. The shapes: Square, Rectangle, Rhombus, Parallelogram.

content.text:
1. First write what each shape has. A square has all sides equal and all angles right angles. A rectangle has opposite sides equal and all angles right angles. A rhombus has all sides equal and no right angles. A parallelogram has opposite sides equal and no right angles. All four have opposite sides equal and opposite angles equal.
[Image: Which Shape Am I?: Ans1: solution]
2. $(1)$: all angles are right angles but the sides are not all equal. A square has all sides equal, so it is left out: Rectangle.
3. $(2)$: all sides are equal but the angles are not all right angles. A square has right angles, so it is left out: Rhombus.
4. $(3)$: opposite angles are equal but the sides do not make a right angle: Rhombus and Parallelogram.
5. $(4)$: two pairs of equal sides and no right angle: Parallelogram and Rhombus.
6. $(5)$: all sides make right angles and are equal: Square.
7. $(6)$: opposite angles equal and opposite sides equal is true of all four shapes: all four.
8. $(7)$: opposite angles equal and the sides make right angles: Square and Rectangle.
9. Check: statements $3$, $4$, $6$ and $7$ name more than one shape, so yes, some statements describe more than one shape.
Answer: $(1)$: Rectangle; $(2)$: Rhombus; $(3)$: Rhombus, Parallelogram; $(4)$: Parallelogram, Rhombus; $(5)$: Square; $(6)$: all four; $(7)$: Square, Rectangle. Yes: $3$, $4$, $6$ and $7$ fit more than one shape.
[Image: Which Shape Am I?: Ans1: solution (continued)]

media.title: Circle Stitcher
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Circle Stitcher
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M4.S20.T20.C97.2D1
- Tool type: Exploration (diameters of a circle, thread designs and compass circles)
- Textbook source: Shapes and Patterns, Play with Circles (two diameters, the four ends joined, a different pair of diameters, another four-sided shape) and Circle Designs (24 points, join 1 to 11, 11 to 2, 2 to 12 and so on; the five-circle flower) (developer only). Practice values: a circle of diameter 12 cm, a thread circle of 10 points (on by 3, back by 2) and one of 8 points (on by 2, back by 1).
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student sees that the four ends of two diameters of a circle always make a rectangle, and threads the points of a circle by a repeating move until the thread is back at the start.
- Out of scope: the length of the circle, drawing a circle without a compass, any rule about angles.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- A wooden workshop table seen from above with a white paper sheet and a brass compass. On the paper is a circle of diameter 12 cm (240 pixels across, the largest thing on the stage) with its centre marked by a red dot. Two diameters cross at the centre, each with a round brass handle at both ends, so 4 points sit on the circle. The activity chooses the stage (compass board, thread board or flower mat).
- Instruction line: "Turn the diameter. Does its length change?" The second diameter's handle pulses once.
2. Scene and Objects
- Compass board: the circle with its two diameters and a length tag on the chosen diameter ("12 cm"). After Join, side tags in whole cm appear, a small square mark sits on each right angle, and a name plate reads "Rectangle" or "Square". Buttons: "Join" and "Right angle" (puts the second diameter at a right angle to the first).
- Thread board: a wooden string-art board with 10, 8 or 24 brass nails round a circle, numbered clockwise from 1 at the top, and four threads (teal, gold, green, plum). A "Move" read-out names the last move by the shorter way round ("on by 10", "back by 9"), a counter reads "lines threaded: 3", and a "Closed" light turns green when the thread is back at point 1.
- Flower mat: coloured paper with the compass, a compass opening handle with a tag in cm ("3 cm"), a "Draw circle" button and a count "circles: 1".
- Goal chip. Bottom buttons (three only): Hint, Reset, Next (locked until the chip is green).
3. Main Interaction
- Compass board: drag a handle to turn its diameter about the centre; both ends move together, so a diameter always goes through the centre. "Join" joins the four ends in order with a dotted line.
- Thread board: tap a nail, then another nail to pull a thread. Tap a colour to change it, the last thread to undo it. The thread may pass a nail that already has a thread.
- Flower mat: drag the opening handle to set the radius; tap the paper to put the pin; "Draw circle" sweeps a full circle round the pin, which marks the centre. Reset clears the board.
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Turn one diameter all the way round. Does its length change?" Goal chip: "Turn a diameter". Setup: the 12 cm circle. Help: guided, a radius tag ("radius 6 cm") is shown. Guess: "As the diameter turns, its length will:" cards "get longer", "get shorter" and "stay the same". Result: the tag keeps reading 12 cm. Why line: "Every diameter goes through the centre and ends on the circle, so it is always 12 cm. The radius is half of it: 12 ÷ 2 = 6 cm."
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Join 1 to 4, then 4 to 2, then 2 to 5. Find the move and go on until you are back at 1." Goal chip: "Closed design". Setup: 10 nails. Help: guided, the Move read-out names each move. Guess: "How many lines will the design have?" cards 10, 15 and 20. Result: the thread goes 1, 4, 2, 5, 3, 6, 4, 7, 5, 8, 6, 9, 7, 10, 8, 1 and the Closed light turns green. Why line: "The move is on by 3, then back by 2. 7 pairs of moves make 14 lines, and 1 more line closes it: 14 + 1 = 15."
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "Join 1 to 3 and 3 to 2. Find the move and go on until you are back at 1." Goal chip: "Closed design". Setup: 8 nails. Guess: "How many lines will the design have?" cards 8, 13 and 16. Result: the thread goes 1, 3, 2, 4, 3, 5, 4, 6, 5, 7, 6, 8, 7, 1. Why line: "The move is on by 2, then back by 1. 6 pairs of moves make 12 lines, and 1 more line closes it: 12 + 1 = 13." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1. Goal line: "Draw a circle with a compass and mark its centre. Draw its diameter. Mark the endpoints of the diameter. Draw another diameter of the circle and mark the endpoints. Now join the four points. What shape is formed? Check the sides of the quadrilateral and the angles obtained." Goal chip: "Join the ends". Setup: compass opening 4 cm. Guess: "The shape will be:" cards "square", "rectangle" and "rhombus". The child draws the circle (radius 4 cm, so the diameter is 4 × 2 = 8 cm), then 2 diameters, then presses Join and reads sides and angles. Result: a rectangle, opposite sides equal, 4 right angles. Why line: "Opposite sides are equal and all four angles are right angles: a rectangle." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 2. Goal line: "Try with a different pair of diameters. What do you notice about the shape that is formed?" Goal chip: "Try 3 pairs". Guess: "When I turn a diameter, what will stay the same?" cards "the sides", "the right angles" and "nothing". The child turns the second diameter to 3 places and joins each time. Result: the sides change, the four angles stay right angles. Why line: "The sides changed, but the four angles are still right angles: a rectangle again." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 3. Goal line: "Is it possible to create a 4-sided shape other than a rectangle through this process?" Goal chip: "Another shape?" Guess: cards "Yes" and "No". The child tries at least 3 pairs of diameters, one of them with "Right angle". Result: No; at the right angle the name plate says "Square". Why line: "Every pair of diameters gives 4 right angles. A square is a rectangle with 4 equal sides, so it is a special rectangle, not a different shape." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 4. Goal line: "Look at the circle given below. It is marked with points 1 to 24. Join points 1 to 11, 11 to 2, 2 to 12, and so on till you reach back at 1." Goal chip: "Back at 1". Setup: 24 nails; the first line 1 to 11 is drawn. Guess: "How many lines will you thread before you are back at 1?" cards 14, 24 and 29. Result: the thread goes 1, 11, 2, 12, 3, 13 and so on to 15, then 1; the Closed light turns green at 29 lines. Why line: "The move is on by 10, then back by 9. 14 pairs of moves make 14 × 2 = 28 lines, and 1 more move on by 10 closes it: 28 + 1 = 29." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 5. Goal line: "Can you think of a way to make a design exactly like the image given here? Try to make it." Goal chip: "Make the flower". Setup: the target flower (5 circles of the same size, one in the middle and four round it, with coloured petals) sits in a corner; compass opening 3 cm. Guess: "How many circles will the flower have?" cards 4, 5 and 6. The child draws one circle, adds 2 diameters at right angles with "Right angle", and draws a circle with the same opening at each of the 4 points. Result: the 5 circles match the target and the petals colour in. Why line: "1 circle in the middle and 4 round it make 1 + 4 = 5 circles of the same size." Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- All diameters of a circle have the same length, two diameters make a rectangle whatever their slant, and a repeated thread move goes round the circle and closes at the start.
- Rules in the child's words: "The four ends of two diameters always make a rectangle." "Find the move, repeat it until you are back at the start, then count the lines."
6. Feedback and Hints
- Wrong answer: red strip, a small shake of the object, and one friendly line naming the mistake and what to look at; no scores, retry is free. Correct: the shape or thread glows green, the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce, the pill gets a tick and Next unlocks.
- Says the shape is a square, or thinks a new pair of diameters could make a different shape -> "Check the 4 sides and the 4 angles again: opposite sides equal and 4 right angles make a rectangle." The sides and right angle marks pulse.
- Taps a nail that does not follow the move -> "The move from 11 is back by 9, so look for point 2." The right nail pulses; no thread is drawn. Stops before the Closed light -> "The thread is not back at the first point yet." The first nail pulses.
- Changes the compass opening between circles -> "The opening changed. Set it back so the circles are the same size." The handle pulses.
- Hint button, 3 levels. (1) Words: "What does the card ask: the shape made by the four ends, or the path of the thread?" (2) Visual clue: the side lengths show, or the next nail pulses. (3) Almost the answer: the tool draws the next two threads, or joins the four ends.
- Edge cases: two diameters on top of each other make no shape ("Turn the second diameter away from the first.").
7. Ending
- A star challenge is done when its result in section 4 is reached; the end screen follows when all chips are green.
- End screen: confetti once. "Well done!" Remember: "The four ends of two diameters always make a rectangle." "At a right angle it is a square." "To thread a design, find the move and repeat it until you are back at the start." Think and talk: "What would happen with 12 points, on by 5 and back by 4?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Images: wooden table, white paper, brass compass, brass nails, coloured threads, flower paper (photo cut-outs). Handles, joins, tags and the target flower are code-drawn. No people. English only.

tool_config.idea: Draw two diameters of a circle, join their four ends and check the sides and the angles to see that the shape is always a rectangle, then thread the points of a circle by a repeating move to make a string design that closes when the thread is back at the start.
tool_config.title: Circle Stitcher
tool_config.screen: A compass board and a thread board on the craft table, drawn as a warm 3-D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. Three tabs at the top of the table switch between the Compass board, the Thread board and the Circle design mat. On the Compass board a circle with a diameter of 10 cm and its centre marked is the largest thing on screen. Two diameters pass through the centre and each end of each diameter is a round handle, so four points sit on the circle. Compass board controls: drag a handle to turn its diameter; a Join button that joins the four ends in order with a dotted line; a turn slider that turns the second diameter slowly all the way round; a Right angle snap that puts the second diameter at a right angle to the first. Compass board read-outs: the four side lengths in centimetres, a small square mark on every angle that is a right angle, and a name plate that reads Rectangle or Square. On the Thread board there is a circle with 12 points numbered 1 to 12 (practice values) or a circle with 24 points numbered 1 to 24, as in your maths book, with a tray of four coloured threads: teal, amber, green and reddish purple. Thread board controls: tap one point and then another to pull a thread between them; tap a colour in the tray to change the thread; Undo takes off the last thread. Thread board read-outs: a Move read-out that names the last move, for example on by 10 or back by 9, the number of lines threaded, and a Closed light that turns green when the thread is back at the first point. On the Circle design mat there is a circle with a radius of 3 cm (practice values), its centre marked and two diameters at right angles, so four points sit on the circle. Circle design mat controls: a Compass opening handle that sets the radius of the circle to draw, and a Draw circle button that draws a circle with its centre on the point you tap; read-outs: the compass opening in centimetres and the number of circles drawn. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Check, Hint, Undo, Retry (clears the last lines or the last circle), Reset (clears the board), Back and Next sit in the same places on every card.
feedback: When the four ends are joined, the read-outs show the four sides and the four angles and the tool says, for example: Opposite sides are equal and all four angles are right angles: a rectangle.
When you turn a diameter the sides change and the tool says: The sides changed, the angles are still right angles, so it is still a rectangle.
When the diameters cross at a right angle the name plate says Square and the tool says: All four sides are equal now, a square is a special rectangle.

Each thread draws from one point to the next and the Move read-out names the move, for example: 1 to 11 is on by 10, 11 to 2 is back by 9. A tap on a point that does not follow the move gives a soft amber note such as: The move from 11 is back by 9, so look for point 2.

When the thread is back at the first point the Closed light turns green and the tool shows the number of lines, for example 29 lines. On the design mat the new circle is drawn with its centre on the point you tapped and the tool says: Same opening, same size.
tool_config.done_when: The student has joined two diameters and seen a rectangle, turned a diameter and seen a rectangle again, made a square, threaded a closed design on the 12-point circle, answered the book's two questions and threaded the 24 points back to point 1.

challenges: Card 1: on the Compass board drag the handles to make two diameters and press Join. Read the sides and the angles. What shape is it? Answer: a rectangle. Opposite sides are equal and all four angles are right angles.

Card 2: turn the second diameter with the slider and watch the read-outs. What changes and what stays the same? Answer: the side lengths change, but the four angles stay right angles and the name plate stays Rectangle.
Card 3: press Right angle snap. What shape is it now? Answer: a square. All four sides are equal and all four angles are right angles. A square is a special rectangle.

Card 4 (practice values): on the Thread board with 12 points, join 1 to 4, 4 to 2, 2 to 5 and keep going until you are back at 1. What is the move, and how many lines did you thread? Answer: on by 3, then back by 2, and 19 lines.

Card 5 (practice values): on the Circle design mat set the compass opening to 3 cm, the radius of the circle, and draw a circle with its centre on one of the 4 points. What do you see? Answer: a new circle of the same size that passes through the centre of the first circle.

Challenge: 'Is it possible to create a 4-sided shape other than a rectangle through this process?' Turn the diameters into as many positions as you like before you answer. Answer: no. The shape is always a rectangle. When the two diameters cross at a right angle it is a square, which is a special rectangle.

Challenge: 'Look at the circle given below. It is marked with points 1 to 24. Join points 1 to 11, 11 to 2, 2 to 12, and so on till you reach back at 1.' Answer: 29 lines. The thread goes on by 10, then back by 9, and it is back at 1 after 29 lines.

hint_ladder.text: What does the card ask: the shape made by the four ends, or the path of the thread? Look at what is on the board.
For the diameters, check the sides and then the angles of the shape. For the thread, find the move from the first two lines.
Turn one diameter a little and check again: what changes and what stays the same? For the thread, 1 to 11 is on by 10 and 11 to 2 is back by 9.
The tool joins the four ends and shows the read-outs: opposite sides equal and four right angles. For the thread it draws 1 to 11 and 11 to 2, and you carry on: 2 to 12 is on by 10 again.

student_does: Look at the 12-point circle from the video, where the thread goes 1, 5, 2, 6, 3, 7 and on. Say the move: on by how many, then back by how many?

On the Compass board draw two diameters, join the ends and read the sides and the angles, turn one diameter and look again, then make the diameters cross at a right angle. Then thread a 12-point circle by a move of your own and try the compass on the design mat.

The book's own questions. Is it possible to create a 4-sided shape other than a rectangle through this process? Then thread the 24 points: join points 1 to 11, 11 to 2, 2 to 12, and so on till you reach back at 1.

media.instructions_for_student: The student sees that the four ends of two diameters always make a rectangle, and threads points round a circle by a repeating move until the thread returns to the start.

media.title: Two diameters and the shape they make
media.context: Concept image for Two Diameters Make a Rectangle. It shows the concept's own circle of diameter 10 cm and not a figure from your maths book.
media.composition: Two equal circles side by side. The left one has two slanted diameters and a rectangle; the right one has two diameters at right angles and a square. Names and sizes sit under the circles.
media.description: A circle of diameter 10 cm with two diameters joined into a rectangle, and a second circle with two diameters at right angles joined into a square, each with right angle marks.
media.source_figure: A circle with two diameters and the four ends joined into a rectangle.
media.teaching_notes: Point at the centre first: both diameters pass through it, so the four ends are all the same distance from it. The slip to watch is expecting a kite or any other four-sided shape.

media.teaching_notes: Predict first: draw two diameters of a circle and join their four ends. What shape do you get? Are its angles right angles? A diameter is a line from one side of the circle to the other that passes through the centre. Every diameter of a circle has the same length, and the radius is half of it. Two diameters cross at the centre. All four ends are the same distance from the centre. Join the four ends in order and check. Opposite sides are equal and all four angles are right angles: a rectangle. Turn one diameter and join again. The sides change, but the shape is still a rectangle. If the two diameters cross at a right angle, all four sides are equal: a square, which is a special rectangle. Rule: the four ends of two diameters always make a rectangle. 1. The diameter is 10 cm, so the radius is half of it: 10 ÷ 2 = 5 cm. 2. Draw one diameter and a second diameter. Both go through the centre, so both are 10 cm long. 3. Join the four ends in order. The shape has 4 sides: it is a quadrilateral. 4. Check the sides: opposite sides are equal. 5. Check the angles: all four are right angles. Opposite sides equal and four right angles: a rectangle. 6. Now turn the second diameter until it crosses the first one at a right angle. All four sides come out equal: a square. A square is a special rectangle. 7. Check: the four ends are all 5 cm from the centre and the two diameters are 10 cm each, so every pair of diameters gives a rectangle. Answer: The radius is 5 cm. Two diameters joined at their ends make a rectangle. If they cross at a right angle it is a square, a special rectangle

media.teaching_notes: Predict first: a circle has 12 points numbered 1 to 12. You join 1 to 5, then 5 to 2, then 2 to 6, and keep going. Does the thread ever come back to 1? Look for the move. 1 to 5 goes on by 4. 5 to 2 goes back by 3. 2 to 6 goes on by 4 again. Keep the same moves: on by 4, back by 3, on by 4, back by 3. Each pair of moves goes on by 1 in all, so the thread starts a little further round each time. When you pass 12, the numbers start again from 1. From 9, going on by 4 takes you to 10, 11, 12 and then 1. The thread is back at 1 and the design is closed. Now count the lines. Rule: find the move, repeat it until the thread is back at the start, then count the lines. 1. Find the move: 1 to 5 is on by 4, 5 to 2 is back by 3, 2 to 6 is on by 4. 2. Keep the same moves: on by 4, back by 3, on by 4, back by 3. 3. Write the points in order: 1, 5, 2, 6, 3, 7, 4, 8, 5, 9, 6, 10, 7, 11, 8, 12, 9. From 9 go on by 4: 10, 11, 12, then 1. The thread is back at 1. 4. Count the lines: each line joins a point to the next one in the list. The list has 18 points with the last 1, so there are 18 − 1 = 17 lines. 5. Check: 8 pairs of moves (on by 4, back by 3) use 16 lines, and one last move on by 4 closes the design, so 8 × 2 + 1 = 17 lines. Answer: 17 lines. The path is 1, 5, 2, 6, 3, 7, 4, 8, 5, 9, 6, 10, 7, 11, 8, 12, 9, 1

content.text:
1. Predict first: draw two diameters of a circle and join their four ends. What shape do you get? Are its angles right angles?
2. A diameter is a line from one side of the circle to the other that passes through the centre. Every diameter of a circle has the same length, and the radius is half of it.
3. Two diameters cross at the centre. All four ends are the same distance from the centre.
4. Join the four ends in order and check. Opposite sides are equal and all four angles are right angles: a rectangle.
5. Turn one diameter and join again. The sides change, but the shape is still a rectangle.
6. If the two diameters cross at a right angle, all four sides are equal: a square, which is a special rectangle.
7. Rule: the four ends of two diameters always make a rectangle.

content.text:
Worked example: A circle has a diameter of 10 cm. Draw two diameters and join their four ends. What is the radius? What shape is formed? What shape is formed when the two diameters cross at a right angle?
{{DIAGRAM:M4.S20.T20.C95.IMG2}}
1. The diameter is 10 cm, so the radius is half of it: 10 ÷ 2 = 5 cm.
2. Draw one diameter and a second diameter. Both go through the centre, so both are 10 cm long.
3. Join the four ends in order. The shape has 4 sides: it is a quadrilateral.
4. Check the sides: opposite sides are equal.
5. Check the angles: all four are right angles. Opposite sides equal and four right angles: a rectangle.
6. Now turn the second diameter until it crosses the first one at a right angle. All four sides come out equal: a square. A square is a special rectangle.
7. Check: the four ends are all 5 cm from the centre and the two diameters are 10 cm each, so every pair of diameters gives a rectangle.
Answer: The radius is 5 cm. Two diameters joined at their ends make a rectangle. If they cross at a right angle it is a square, a special rectangle

content.text:
1. Predict first: a circle has 12 points numbered 1 to 12. You join 1 to 5, then 5 to 2, then 2 to 6, and keep going. Does the thread ever come back to 1?
2. Look for the move. 1 to 5 goes on by 4. 5 to 2 goes back by 3. 2 to 6 goes on by 4 again.
3. Keep the same moves: on by 4, back by 3, on by 4, back by 3. Each pair of moves goes on by 1 in all, so the thread starts a little further round each time.
4. When you pass 12, the numbers start again from 1. From 9, going on by 4 takes you to 10, 11, 12 and then 1.
5. The thread is back at 1 and the design is closed. Now count the lines.
6. Rule: find the move, repeat it until the thread is back at the start, then count the lines.

content.text:
Worked example: A circle has 12 points numbered 1 to 12 round it. Join 1 to 5, 5 to 2, 2 to 6, 6 to 3, and so on until you reach 1 again. How many lines do you draw?
{{DIAGRAM:M4.S20.T20.C96.IMG2}}
1. Find the move: 1 to 5 is on by 4, 5 to 2 is back by 3, 2 to 6 is on by 4.
2. Keep the same moves: on by 4, back by 3, on by 4, back by 3.
3. Write the points in order: 1, 5, 2, 6, 3, 7, 4, 8, 5, 9, 6, 10, 7, 11, 8, 12, 9. From 9 go on by 4: 10, 11, 12, then 1. The thread is back at 1.
4. Count the lines: each line joins a point to the next one in the list. The list has 18 points with the last 1, so there are 18 − 1 = 17 lines.
5. Check: 8 pairs of moves (on by 4, back by 3) use 16 lines, and one last move on by 4 closes the design, so 8 × 2 + 1 = 17 lines.
Answer: 17 lines. The path is 1, 5, 2, 6, 3, 7, 4, 8, 5, 9, 6, 10, 7, 11, 8, 12, 9, 1

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M4.S21.T21.C99.IMG1}}
1. Draw a circle with a compass. Say the radius is $4\text{ cm}$, so the diameter is $4 \times 2 = 8\text{ cm}$. Mark the centre.
2. Draw one diameter through the centre and mark its two ends.
3. Draw a second diameter through the centre and mark its two ends. You now have four points.
4. Join the four points in order round the circle. The shape has $4$ sides.
[Image: Play with Circles: Ans1: solution]
5. Look at the sides: opposite sides are equal.
6. Look at the angles: all four are right angles.
7. Check: opposite sides equal and four right angles are both true, so the shape is a rectangle.
Answer: A rectangle: opposite sides are equal and all four angles are right angles.
[Image: Play with Circles: Ans1: solution (continued)]

content.text: Is it possible to create a $4$-sided shape other than a rectangle through this process?

content.book_number: Play with Circles: another four-sided shape

content.publication_text: Is it possible to create a $4$-sided shape other than a rectangle through this process?

content.text:
1. Every pair of diameters gives a rectangle: opposite sides equal and four right angles.
2. Turn one diameter all the way round the centre. The four ends always make a rectangle, and never a different $4$-sided shape.
3. When the two diameters cross at a right angle, all four sides are equal: a square. A square is a special rectangle, so it is not a different shape.
4. Check: in every try the four angles were right angles, so the shape is a rectangle.
Answer: No. The shape is always a rectangle. When the diameters cross at a right angle it is a square, which is a special rectangle.

{{DIAGRAM:M4.S22.T22.C105.IMG1}}
1. Find the move: $1$ to $11$ goes on by $10$. $11$ to $2$ goes back by $9$. $2$ to $12$ goes on by $10$ again.
2. Keep the same moves, on by $10$ and back by $9$: $1$, $11$, $2$, $12$, $3$, $13$, $4$, $14$, $5$, $15$, $6$, $16$, $7$, $17$, $8$, $18$, $9$, $19$, $10$, $20$, $11$, $21$, $12$, $22$, $13$, $23$, $14$, $24$, $15$.
3. From $15$ go on by $10$: $16$, $17$ and on to $24$, then $1$. The thread is back at $1$.
[Image: Circle Designs: Ans1: solution]
4. Count the lines: $14$ pairs of moves make $14 \times 2 = 28$ lines, and the last move on by $10$ makes $1$ more line, so $28 + 1 = 29$.
5. Check: the list of points has $30$ places with the last $1$, so there are $30 - 1 = 29$ lines.
Answer: $29$ lines. The thread goes on by $10$, back by $9$, and is back at $1$ after $29$ lines.
[Image: Circle Designs: Ans1: solution (continued)]

media.title: Cube Lab
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Cube Lab
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M4.S23.T23.C110.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity (find opposite faces, fold a net, count painted and removed small cubes)
- Textbook source: Shapes and Patterns, Cube Connections: the three views of a cube to draw on a net, the three cube frames (3 by 3 by 3, 4 by 4 by 4, 5 by 5 by 5) and the 27 small cubes that Nisha paints red (developer only). Practice values: a fruit cube, a painted 5 by 5 by 5 cube, and a 6 by 6 by 6 frame with a tunnel 4 wide.
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student finds which faces of a cube are opposite from views of it, places pictures on a net, and counts how many small cubes of a painted big cube have three, two, one or no painted faces, and how many are removed from a frame.
- Out of scope: other solids, how much space a cube holds, any formula for a cube.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- A carpenter's workbench seen from above with a big wooden cube in the middle, the largest thing on the stage. Its faces carry apple, banana, cherry, grape, lemon and a plain face. Two small view cards stand along the bottom edge: "View A" and "View B", each showing the cube from a corner.
- Instruction line: "Tap View A and View B. Which face is opposite the banana?" The View A card pulses once.
2. Scene and Objects
- Benches (the stage changes with the activity): the cube bench (cube, view cards, a net of 6 empty squares and a tray of 6 picture tiles), the paint bench (a stack of small wooden cubes, a red paint tin and 4 tally boxes "3 faces painted", "2 faces", "1 face", "no face") and the frame bench (a stack of small cubes, a tunnel width stepper and counters "removed" and "left").
- Net: a cardboard cross, a row of 4 squares with one square above and one below the third. "Fold" folds it into a cube with the pictures outside; "Unfold" opens it. Each view card shows 3 faces seen at once (top, left, right) with a match light after Fold: "match" (green) or "not yet" (orange, with the reason).
- Goal chip. Bottom buttons (three only): Hint, Reset, Next (locked until the chip is green).
3. Main Interaction
- Drag the cube to turn it; tap a view card to set the cube to that view (a line names the 3 faces seen). Net: drag a tile onto a square, tap it to take it back.
- Paint bench: "Paint" paints the outside red; "Peel" takes off one outer layer; tap a small cube to lift it out, then tap how many of its faces are painted (cards 0 to 3). All cubes of that kind then glow and move into the matching box together.
- Frame bench: set the tunnel width (at most 2 less than the cube width), then "Cut tunnels" removes a square tunnel through every pair of opposite faces. Reset clears the bench.
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Tap View A and View B. Which face is opposite the banana?" Goal chip: "Opposite the banana". Setup: the fruit cube. View A: apple on top, banana left, cherry right. View B: apple on top, cherry left, grape right. Help: guided, the faces seen are named. Guess: "Opposite the banana is:" cards "cherry", "grape" and "lemon". Result: the grape. Why line: "The banana and the grape both touch the apple and the cherry, so the grape is opposite the banana."
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Put the banana and the grape on the net so that they fold to opposite faces." Goal chip: "Fold the net". Setup: the net and 2 tiles, banana and grape. Help: guided, the squares of a straight row are numbered. Guess: "On the net the banana and the grape will be:" cards "next to each other", "with 1 square between them in a row" and "in different rows". Result: with 1 square between them in a row (or one above and one below the third square), Fold shows the match light "opposite". Why line: "In a straight row of 3 squares, the first and the third fold up to opposite faces."
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "Paint the 5 by 5 by 5 cube, peel it and sort the small cubes." Goal chip: "Sort 125 cubes". Guess: "Which box will hold the most cubes?" cards "3 faces", "2 faces", "1 face" and "no face". The child paints, peels, and lifts one cube of each kind. Result: the boxes show 8, 36, 54 and 27. Why line: "Edges 12 × 3 = 36, face middles 6 × 9 = 54, inside 3 × 3 × 3 = 27, corners 8, and 8 + 36 + 54 + 27 = 125." Help: independent.
- Activity 4 (independent). Goal line: "Cut a tunnel 4 wide through the 6 by 6 by 6 cube. How many small cubes are removed?" Goal chip: "Cut the frame". Setup: 216 small cubes. Guess: "Removed:" cards 56, 160 and 216. Result: the counters read removed 160 and left 56. Why line: "6 × 6 × 6 = 216. What is left is the 8 corners and 4 cubes on each of the 12 edges: 8 + 12 × 4 = 56, so 216 − 56 = 160 are removed." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1. Goal line: "Here are three views of a cube. Can you draw them on the net in the correct order?" Goal chip: "3 views on the net". Setup: View 1 top diamond (green on purple), left circle (orange on blue), right cross (red on cream); View 2 top diamond, left cross, right star (blue on pink); View 3 top brown (a plain face), left circle, right cross. Tray: diamond, circle, star, brown and 2 crosses. Guess: "Which face is opposite the brown face?" cards "diamond", "circle" and "star". The child places the 6 tiles and presses Fold; each view card shows its light. Any placement whose folded cube shows all 3 views is accepted (24 work). Result: all 3 lights turn green; for example a row of brown, circle, diamond and star, with a cross above and a cross below the diamond square. Why line: "The diamond and the brown face both touch the circle and the cross, so they are opposite. So are the circle and the star." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 2. Goal line: "Nisha has glued 27 small cubes together to make a large solid cube. She paints the large cube red. How many of the original small cubes have (a) three faces painted red? (b) two faces painted red? (c) one face painted red? (d) no faces painted red?" Goal chip: "Sort 27 cubes". Setup: a 3 by 3 by 3 stack. Guess: a number chip for each of (a) to (d) ((a) 4, 8 or 12; (b) 6, 12 or 24; (c) 1, 6 or 9; (d) 0, 1 or 8); the tool then paints, peels and sorts the cubes. Result: (a) 8, (b) 12, (c) 6, (d) 1. Why line: "8 + 12 + 6 + 1 = 27, all the small cubes." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 3. Goal line: "Here are some big solid cube frames. How many small cubes have been removed from each cube? (a) (b) (c)" Goal chip: "3 frames". Setup: solid cubes of 3 by 3 by 3, 4 by 4 by 4 and 5 by 5 by 5, each beside the same cube with a square tunnel through every pair of opposite faces (tunnels 1, 2 and 3 wide). Guess: a number chip for each: (a) 7, 20 or 27; (b) 16, 32 or 64; (c) 44, 81 or 125; the removed cubes then lift out and are counted. Result: (a) 7, (b) 32, (c) 81. Why line: "Cubes left: 8 + 12 × 1 = 20 of 27, 8 + 12 × 2 = 32 of 64, 8 + 12 × 3 = 44 of 125. So 27 − 20 = 7, 64 − 32 = 32 and 125 − 44 = 81 are removed." Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- Faces seen together touch each other, so opposite faces are never in one view. Small cubes sort into corners, edges, face middles and the cube inside, and together they make the whole.
- Rules in the child's words: "Two faces that touch the same two touching faces are opposite." "Corners 3 painted faces, edges 2, face middles 1, inside none."
6. Feedback and Hints
- Wrong answer: red strip, a small shake of the object, and one friendly line naming the mistake and what to look at; no scores, retry is free. Correct: the match light turns green, the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce, the pill gets a tick and Next unlocks.
- Names two faces seen in one view as opposite -> "Faces you see together touch each other, so they cannot be opposite." The faces pulse.
- Net does not match a view -> "View 2 does not match yet. Look at what touches the diamond face." The two faces pulse.
- Says no small cube has no paint (d = 0) -> "Peel off the outer layer. Is there a cube in the middle? Paint cannot reach it." The inside cube glows after Peel.
- Sorts a corner cube into the 2 faces box -> "A corner cube touches 3 faces of the big cube. Count its painted faces." The cube slides back. Gives the cubes left instead of removed -> "Removed and left must make the whole cube." The counters pulse.
- Hint button, 3 levels. (1) Words: "Which faces do you see together in one view? They touch each other." Or: "How many outside faces does this cube touch?" (2) Visual clue: the two faces that touch the same pair glow, or the corner cubes glow. (3) Almost the answer: the diamond tile is placed in the third square of the row, or the outer layer is peeled off.
- Edge cases: the 3 by 3 by 3 cube has exactly 1 cube with no paint; the two crosses are identical tiles.
7. Ending
- A star challenge is done when its result in section 4 is reached; the end screen follows when all chips are green.
- End screen: confetti once. "Well done!" Remember: "Two faces that touch the same two touching faces are opposite." "In a painted cube, corners have 3 painted faces, edges 2, face middles 1, and the cube inside none." "Removed and left make all the small cubes." Think and talk: "In a 6 by 6 by 6 painted cube, how many small cubes have no paint?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Images: carpenter's workbench; big and small wooden cubes (3D); cardboard net; red paint tin, brush and saw (photo cut-outs). The face pictures (apple, banana, cherry, grape, lemon, diamond, circle, star, cross) are flat drawings. Boxes, view cards and chips are code-drawn. No people. English only.

tool_config.idea: Turn a cube and fold a net to say which faces are opposite, then paint and remove small cubes to count how many have three, two, one or no painted faces and how many are left in a cube frame.
tool_config.title: Cube Lab
tool_config.screen: A cube, a net and small cubes on the craft table, drawn as a warm 3-D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. Three tabs at the top of the table switch between the Cube and net bench, the Paint bench and the Frame bench. On the Cube and net bench a big cube with a picture on each face is the largest thing on screen: a sun, a moon, a heart, a leaf, a star and a plain face. On the left sits a row of view cards: View 1 and View 2 from the video, and the three views of the book's question. On the right is a cross-shaped net of 6 empty squares, a row of 4 squares with one square above and one below the third square, with a tray of 6 picture tiles under it; the sixth tile can be set to show any one of the pictures. Cube and net controls: drag the cube to turn it; tap a view card to set the cube to that view; drag a picture tile onto a net square and tap the turn button to turn the picture; Fold folds the net into a cube and Unfold opens it. Cube and net read-outs: a line that names the three faces you can see, and, after Fold, a match light on each view card that says match or not yet with the reason. On the Paint bench a stack of small cubes (5 by 5 by 5 for practice values, 3 by 3 by 3 for the book's question) has a Paint button that paints the outside red, a Peel button that takes off one outer layer at a time, and a tap on any small cube lifts it out into one of four tally boxes: three painted faces, two, one and none. Paint bench read-outs: the number of small cubes in the stack and the number in each tally box. On the Frame bench a stack of small cubes (6 by 6 by 6, practice values) has a tunnel width control and a Cut tunnels button that removes a square tunnel through every pair of opposite faces; read-outs: the cubes removed and the cubes left. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Check, Hint, Undo, Retry (unfolds the net or puts back the last cubes), Reset (clears the bench), Back and Next sit in the same places on every card.
feedback: After Fold the tool says which views match, for example: View 1 matches. In View 2 the leaf and the moon should be next to the sun: look at what touches the sun.
When you turn the cube the tool names the faces you see and says: Faces you see together touch each other, so they cannot be opposite.
Both the heart and the moon touch the sun and the leaf: they are opposite. The tool shows this when the two views are set one after the other.

On the Paint bench a small cube lifted into the wrong tally box slides back with a clue such as: Count the painted faces of this cube. How many outside faces does it touch? The cube hidden in the middle has none.

On the Frame bench the tool says how many were removed and how many are left, and a count that does not add up gets a soft amber note, for example: Removed and left must make 216. A wrong answer is never shown in red.

challenges: Card 1: tap View 1 and View 2 and turn the cube. Which face is opposite the heart? Answer: the moon. Both the heart and the moon touch the sun and the leaf.

Card 2 (practice values): drop the six pictures on the net: the heart, the leaf, the moon and the plain face along the row of 4 squares from left to right, the sun above the third square and the star below it. Press Fold. Which faces are opposite? Answer: the cube matches View 1 and View 2. The heart and the moon have one square between them in the row, so they are opposite, and so are the leaf and the plain face. The sun above and the star below the third square are opposite too.

Card 3 (practice values): on the Paint bench take the 5 by 5 by 5 stack, press Paint, then Peel and sort the small cubes. How many have three, two, one and no painted faces? Answer: 8, 36, 54 and 27, because 12 × 3 = 36, 6 × 9 = 54 and 3 × 3 × 3 = 27, and 8 + 36 + 54 + 27 = 125.

Card 4 (practice values): on the Frame bench take the 6 by 6 by 6 stack and cut a tunnel 4 by 4 through every pair of opposite faces. How many small cubes are removed? Answer: 160. What is left is the 8 corners and 4 cubes on each of the 12 edges, 8 + 12 × 4 = 56, and 6 × 6 × 6 = 216, so 216 − 56 = 160 are removed.

Challenge: 'Here are three views of a cube. Can you draw them on the net in the correct order?' Answer: the diamond face is opposite the brown face, the circle face is opposite the star face, and the cross is on two opposite faces. Your net may differ if it keeps the same opposite faces.

hint_ladder.text: Which faces can you see together in one view? Faces seen together touch each other. For small cubes, ask how many outside faces a cube touches.
Opposite faces never touch and are never seen together. Look for two faces that touch the same two touching faces. For small cubes, sort them: corner, edge, face middle, inside.
Turn the cube to the view you need and name the faces you see. For small cubes, count the corners, then the cubes on each edge, then the cubes in the middle of a face, then the cubes inside.

The tool places one picture on the net, the diamond in the third square of the row, so you can see how the other pictures fit round it. For small cubes it peels off the outer layer so you can count the cubes left inside.

media.teaching_notes: Predict first: in one view of a cube the heart touches the sun and the leaf. In another view the moon touches the sun and the leaf. Which face is opposite the heart? Faces that you see together in one view touch each other, so they are not opposite. Opposite faces are never seen together. The heart touches the sun and the leaf. The moon also touches the sun and the leaf. The sun and the leaf touch each other along one edge, and the two faces at the two ends of that edge are opposite. So the heart is opposite the moon. A net is a cube cut open and laid flat: 6 squares joined by their sides. In a straight row of 3 squares, the first and the third fold up to opposite faces. Rule: two faces that both touch the same two touching faces are opposite each other. 1. View 1: the heart touches the sun and the leaf. 2. View 2: the moon touches the sun and the leaf. 3. So the heart and the moon both touch the same two faces, the sun and the leaf. 4. The sun and the leaf touch each other along one edge. The two faces at the two ends of that edge are opposite each other, and they are the heart and the moon. 5. So the heart is opposite the moon. 6. Check: opposite faces are never seen together. The heart is in View 1 and the moon is in View 2, and they never appear in the same view. Answer: The moon is opposite the heart

topics.summary: Two faces that touch the same two touching faces are opposite. A big painted cube has corner cubes with three painted faces, edge cubes with two, face middles with one and an inside with none.

content.text:
1. Predict first: in one view of a cube the heart touches the sun and the leaf. In another view the moon touches the sun and the leaf. Which face is opposite the heart?
2. Faces that you see together in one view touch each other, so they are not opposite. Opposite faces are never seen together.
3. The heart touches the sun and the leaf. The moon also touches the sun and the leaf. The sun and the leaf touch each other along one edge, and the two faces at the two ends of that edge are opposite.
4. So the heart is opposite the moon.
5. A net is a cube cut open and laid flat: 6 squares joined by their sides. In a straight row of 3 squares, the first and the third fold up to opposite faces.
6. Rule: two faces that both touch the same two touching faces are opposite each other.

concepts.concept_name: Faces of a Cube and Its Net

content.text:
1. Predict first: a big cube is made of 4 × 4 × 4 small cubes and its whole outside is painted. How many small cubes have no paint at all?
2. Sort the small cubes by where they sit: corners, edges, face middles and inside.
3. A corner cube touches 3 faces of the big cube, so it has 3 painted faces. A cube has 8 corners.
4. An edge cube that is not a corner has 2 painted faces. Each edge has 4 − 2 = 2 of them, and a cube has 12 edges.
5. A face middle cube has 1 painted face. Each face has 2 × 2 = 4 of them, and a cube has 6 faces.
6. An inside cube touches no outside face. Take away the outer layer all round and 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 cubes are left inside.
7. Rule: corners 3 faces, edges 2 faces, face middles 1 face, inside none, and the four counts add up to all the small cubes.

media.teaching_notes: 1. Name the pictures: a green diamond on purple, an orange circle on blue, a red cross on cream, a blue star on pink, and a plain brown face. 2. Faces seen together in one view touch each other, so they are next to each other and not opposite. 3. The diamond face and the brown face both touch the circle face and the cross face, so the diamond is opposite the brown face. 4. The circle face and the star face both touch the diamond face and the cross face, so the circle is opposite the star. 5. A cube has 6 faces: diamond, brown, circle, star and two more. The third view shows a cross next to the circle and the brown face, so the cross must be on two opposite faces. 6. Draw the net: a row of 4 squares with the brown face, the circle, the diamond and the star from left to right, then a cross above the diamond square and a cross below it. Turn each picture so it looks as it does in the views. 7. Check: in the row, brown and diamond have one square between them, and so do circle and star, so each pair is opposite. The two crosses are above and below the diamond square, so they are opposite too. Answer: Sample answer: a net with a row of 4 squares, brown, circle, diamond, star, and a cross above and below the diamond square. Your net may differ if it keeps the same opposite faces.

Answer: Sample answer: a net with a row of $4$ squares, brown, circle, diamond, star, and a cross above and below the diamond square. Your net may differ if it keeps the same opposite faces.

content.text:
1. $(a)$: the cube is $3$ by $3$ by $3$, so it has $3 \times 3 \times 3 = 27$ small cubes.
2. A square tunnel goes through the middle of every pair of opposite faces. What is left is the $8$ corners and $1$ cube on each of the $12$ edges: $8 + 12 \times 1 = 20$. Removed: $27 - 20 = 7$.
[Image: Cube Connections: Ans2: solution]
3. $(b)$: the cube is $4$ by $4$ by $4$, so it has $4 \times 4 \times 4 = 64$ small cubes. Left: the $8$ corners and $2$ cubes on each of the $12$ edges: $8 + 12 \times 2 = 32$. Removed: $64 - 32 = 32$.
4. $(c)$: the cube is $5$ by $5$ by $5$, so it has $5 \times 5 \times 5 = 125$ small cubes. Left: the $8$ corners and $3$ cubes on each of the $12$ edges: $8 + 12 \times 3 = 44$. Removed: $125 - 44 = 81$.
5. Check: $20 + 7 = 27$, $32 + 32 = 64$ and $44 + 81 = 125$.
Answer: $(a)$: $7$ small cubes; $(b)$: $32$ small cubes; $(c)$: $81$ small cubes.
[Image: Cube Connections: Ans2: solution (continued)]
steps: (a): the cube is 3 by 3 by 3, so it has 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 small cubes.
A square tunnel goes through the middle of every pair of opposite faces. What is left is the 8 corners and 1 cube on each of the 12 edges: 8 + 12 × 1 = 20. Removed: 27 − 20 = 7.
(b): the cube is 4 by 4 by 4, so it has 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 small cubes. Left: the 8 corners and 2 cubes on each of the 12 edges: 8 + 12 × 2 = 32. Removed: 64 − 32 = 32.
(c): the cube is 5 by 5 by 5, so it has 5 × 5 × 5 = 125 small cubes. Left: the 8 corners and 3 cubes on each of the 12 edges: 8 + 12 × 3 = 44. Removed: 125 − 44 = 81.

6. Check: $8 + 12 + 6 + 1 = 27$, all the small cubes.
Answer: $(a)$: $8$; $(b)$: $12$; $(c)$: $6$; $(d)$: $1$.
[Image: Cube Connections: Ans3: solution (continued)]

media.title: Solid Counter
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Solid Counter
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M4.S27.T27.C123.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity (tick faces, vertices and edges of solids and count the edges by halving)
- Textbook source: Shapes and Patterns, Icosahedron and Dodecahedron: what the names mean, the shapes of the faces, the faces at a vertex, the number of edges, other solids with faces that look the same, and building solids with straws and clay (developer only). Practice values: a tent-shaped solid with 2 triangle faces and 3 rectangle faces.
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student counts the faces, vertices and edges of a solid by ticking each one once, and finds the edges by adding the sides of all the faces and halving, because each edge is a side of 2 faces.
- Out of scope: names of other solids, how much space a solid holds, any rule linking the numbers of faces, vertices and edges.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- A clay modeller's shelf. A round wooden turntable carries a tent-shaped card model (2 triangle faces at the ends and 3 rectangle faces); it is the largest thing on the stage. Beside it lie a lump of clay and a few straws. Along the bottom edge four model cards stand in a row: "Tent", "Icosahedron", "Dodecahedron" and "Cube".
- Instruction line: "Turn the tent and tick each face once."
- The turntable handle pulses once.
2. Scene and Objects
- Models (photo-style card and clay solids): the tent (equilateral triangle ends, 3 equal rectangle faces); the icosahedron (20 triangle faces, 12 vertices); the dodecahedron (12 pentagon faces, 20 vertices); the cube (6 square faces, 8 vertices); for Star Challenge 5 also a matchbox (6 rectangle faces of 3 different sizes).
- Mode switch: round buttons "Faces", "Vertices" and "Edges" choose what a tap ticks. A tick is a gold mark on a face, a gold ring on a vertex or a gold line on an edge. Counters: "faces ticked", "vertices ticked", "edges ticked". A line says if anything is unticked ("One face is hidden at the back").
- Tally strip under the model: adds the sides of every ticked face, for example "2 × 3 + 3 × 4 = 18", with a "Halve" button on it.
- Build bench (Star Challenge 6): 12 straws, 8 clay balls, and a drawing of a cube frame with 8 dotted rings (corners) and 12 dotted lines (edges), or of a tent frame with 6 rings and 9 lines.
- Goal chip. Bottom buttons (three only): Hint, Reset, Next (locked until the chip is green).
3. Main Interaction
- Drag the turntable to turn the solid; tap a model card to put that model on it. Tap a face, vertex or edge in the chosen mode to tick it; tap again to take the tick off. A tap on a vertex also lights the faces that touch it and shows their number.
- "Tally" needs all faces ticked first. Ticks stay on a solid until Reset clears them.
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Turn the tent and tick each face once. How many faces are there?" Goal chip: "Tick all faces". Setup: the tent, mode Faces. Help: guided, faces are numbered as ticked and their shapes shown. Guess: "How many faces will the tent have?" cards 4, 5 and 6. Result: after 5 ticks the line says "All faces are counted, none is missed". Why line: "2 triangles and 3 rectangles: 2 + 3 = 5 faces."
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Tap one vertex. How many faces meet there? Then tick all the vertices." Goal chip: "Tick all vertices". Setup: the tent, mode Vertices. Help: guided, the faces at the tapped vertex glow. Guess: "How many faces meet at a vertex?" cards 2, 3 and 4. Result: 3 faces meet at every vertex and the tent has 6 vertices. Why line: "At each vertex 1 triangle and 2 rectangles meet: 3 faces. Each triangle has 3 vertices, and 3 + 3 = 6 vertices."
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "How many edges does the tent have? Press Tally, then Halve." Goal chip: "Count the edges". Setup: the tent with all faces ticked. Guess: "The tent has this many edges:" cards 9, 12 and 18. Result: Tally reads 2 × 3 + 3 × 4 = 18 and Halve makes it 9. Why line: "2 triangles with 3 sides and 3 rectangles with 4 sides: 2 × 3 + 3 × 4 = 18 sides. Every edge is a side of 2 faces, so 18 ÷ 2 = 9 edges." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1. Goal line: "What do these names mean? Once you count their faces, you will know." Goal chip: "Count the faces". Setup: the icosahedron and the dodecahedron, mode Faces. Guess: "Which solid has more faces?" cards "icosahedron" and "dodecahedron". The child ticks every face of each. Result: 20 faces and 12 faces; name cards light up "icosa = 20" and "dodeca = 12". Why line: "Icosa means 20 and dodeca means 12, and hedron means face. The names say how many faces." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 2. Goal line: "What shapes do you see in an icosahedron and a dodecahedron? Do all the faces look the same?" Goal chip: "Name the faces". Setup: both solids; shape cards "triangle", "square", "pentagon" and "hexagon". Guess: the child picks a shape card for each solid, then "Yes" or "No" for "all the faces look the same". A tap on a face reads "3 sides" or "5 sides"; a face can be laid over another to compare. Result: icosahedron triangles, dodecahedron pentagons, all faces the same in each. Why line: "Each icosahedron face has 3 sides and each dodecahedron face has 5 sides, and every face of a solid is the same." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 3. Goal line: "How many faces meet at a vertex (point)? Do the same number of faces meet at each vertex?" Goal chip: "Faces at a vertex". Setup: both solids, mode Vertices. Guess: a number card 3, 4, 5 or 6 for each solid. The child taps several vertices of each. Result: 5 faces meet at a vertex of the icosahedron and 3 at a vertex of the dodecahedron, the same at every vertex. Why line: "5 triangles meet at each vertex of the icosahedron, and 3 pentagons meet at each vertex of the dodecahedron." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 4. Goal line: "How many edges do you see? How did you count them such that you do not miss out any edge or count an edge twice?" Goal chip: "Count the edges". Setup: both solids with all faces ticked. Guess: a number card 20, 30 or 60 for each solid. The child presses Tally, then Halve. Result: 30 edges in each solid. Why line: "20 × 3 = 60 sides and 12 × 5 = 60 sides. Every edge is a side of 2 faces, so 60 ÷ 2 = 30 edges." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 5. Goal line: "Can you think of any other solid shapes that have faces that look the same? Do the same number of faces meet at each common vertex?" Goal chip: "Other solids". Setup: a shelf with the cube, the matchbox and the tent. Guess: "Which solid has faces that all look the same?" cards "cube", "matchbox" and "tent". The child lays faces over each other, then taps the vertices of the chosen solid. Result: the cube: 6 faces that are all squares, and 3 faces meet at every vertex. Why line: "All 6 faces of the cube are squares of the same size, and 3 faces meet at each of its 8 vertices." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 6. Goal line: "You can also build some solid shapes using straws or ice-cream sticks and clay or play dough. Which shapes did you make?" Goal chip: "Build a model". Setup: the build bench with two model cards, "Cube frame" and "Tent frame". Guess: "How many straws and clay balls will you need?" with two rows of cards: straws 9, 12 or 24, and clay balls 6, 8 or 12. The child drags clay balls onto the corners and straws onto the edges. Result: the model stands and the line says what was made. Why line (cube): "A cube frame needs 12 straws and 8 balls of clay: 8 balls with 3 straws each make 8 × 3 = 24 straw ends, and 12 straws have 12 × 2 = 24 ends." For the tent frame: 9 straws and 6 balls, and 6 × 3 = 18 ends match 9 × 2 = 18. Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- Ticking each face and vertex once keeps every one counted exactly once. The sides of all the faces counted together count every edge twice, so the edges are half of that total.
- Rules in the child's words: "Tick each one once." "A vertex is a point where faces meet." "Add the sides of all the faces, then halve."
6. Feedback and Hints
- Wrong answer: red strip, a small shake of the object, and one friendly line naming the mistake and what to look at; no scores, retry is free. Correct: the model glows green, the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce, the pill gets a tick and Next unlocks.
- Ticks a face twice -> "This face is already counted." The face pulses.
- Stops with a hidden face -> "One face is still hidden at the back. Turn the solid." The turntable turns to show it.
- Says the edges are the sum of all the sides (60) -> "Each edge is a side of 2 faces, so it was counted twice. Halve the total." The Halve button pulses.
- Says the faces of a matchbox look the same -> "Lay one face over another. Do they match?" The 2 faces slide together.
- Hint button, 3 levels. (1) Words: "What are you counting: faces, vertices or edges? Choose the mode first." (2) Visual clue: the next unticked face, vertex or edge glows. (3) Almost the answer: the tool ticks one face and one edge and starts the sides tally.
- Edge cases: the same number of faces meets at every vertex of a solid (5 for the icosahedron, 3 for the dodecahedron and the cube); a Tally with unticked faces says "Tick all the faces first."
7. Ending
- A star challenge is done when its result in section 4 is reached; the end screen follows when all chips are green.
- End screen: confetti once. "Well done!" Remember: "Tick each face and each vertex once, so none is missed." "A vertex is a point where faces meet." "To count the edges, add the sides of all the faces and halve." Think and talk: "A solid has 8 faces and each face has 3 sides. How many edges does it have?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Images: clay modeller's shelf; wooden turntable; card and clay models of the tent, icosahedron, dodecahedron, cube and matchbox (3D); straws and clay balls (photo cut-outs). Ticks, counters and the tally strip are code-drawn. No people. English only.

tool_config.idea: Tick the faces, vertices and edges of a box and then of the icosahedron and the dodecahedron, one tick for each, and find the number of edges by adding the sides of all the faces and halving, so that nothing is missed and nothing is counted twice.
tool_config.title: Solid Counter
tool_config.screen: A turntable on the craft table with clay models, drawn as a warm 3-D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. The solid on the turntable is the largest thing on screen. Three model cards on the left choose the solid: Box, Icosahedron and Dodecahedron. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: drag the turntable to turn the solid so that every side can be seen; a mode switch with Faces, Vertices and Edges that chooses what a tap ticks; tap a face, a vertex or an edge to tick it with an amber mark and tap it again to take the tick off; a Tally button that opens a strip adding the sides of every ticked face, and a Halve button on that strip; Check, Hint, Undo, Retry (clears the ticks of this card), Reset (clears the solid), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: three counters, faces ticked, vertices ticked and edges ticked; a faces at this vertex read-out that lights up the faces touching a ticked vertex and shows their number; the sides tally, for example 6 faces × 4 sides = 24, and the halved number under it; and a line that says whether any face, vertex or edge is still unticked.
feedback: Each tick turns the face, vertex or edge amber and the counter goes up by one. Ticking the same one again shows a soft amber note: This face is already counted.
A tap on a vertex lights the faces that touch it and says, for example: 5 faces meet at this vertex.
The Tally strip adds the sides of the ticked faces and says, for example: 20 faces with 3 sides is 60. Every edge is counted twice, so halve it: 30 edges.
When every face is ticked the tool says: All 20 faces are counted, none is missed. If one is still unticked it turns the solid to show where it is and says: One face is still hidden at the back.
A wrong count shows a soft amber note and never a red cross; the tool names the number it expected only after the second try.

challenges: Card 1: on the box choose Faces and tap each face once. How many faces are there, and what shape are they? Answer: 6 faces, all rectangles.

Card 2: on the box choose Vertices and tap one vertex, then count all the vertices. How many faces meet at a vertex, and how many vertices are there? Answer: 3 faces meet at every vertex, and the box has 8 vertices.
Card 3: on the box press Tally, then Halve. How many edges does the box have? Answer: 6 × 4 = 24 sides, and 24 ÷ 2 = 12 edges.
Card 4: switch to the icosahedron, choose Faces and tick every face. How many faces, and what shape are they? Answer: 20 faces, all triangles.
Card 5: switch to the dodecahedron, choose Faces and tick every face. How many faces, and what shape are they? Answer: 12 faces, all pentagons.

Challenge: 'How many faces meet at a vertex (point)?' Tap vertices on the icosahedron and on the dodecahedron and compare. Answer: the icosahedron has 5 faces at a vertex and the dodecahedron has 3, and the same number of faces meet at every vertex of each solid.

Challenge: 'How many edges do you see? How did you count them such that you do not miss out any edge or count an edge twice?' Answer: 30 edges in each solid. Add the sides of all the faces, 20 × 3 = 60 for the icosahedron and 12 × 5 = 60 for the dodecahedron, then halve it, because each edge is a side of 2 faces: 60 ÷ 2 = 30.

hint_ladder.text: What are you counting: faces, vertices or edges? Choose the mode first.
Tick each one once and watch the counter, and turn the solid so that no face is hidden. For edges, think about how many faces share each edge.
For the edges, add the sides of all the faces, then halve it. Each edge is a side of how many faces?
The tool ticks one face and then one edge and starts the sides tally, so you can see the method: add the sides of the faces, then halve.

media.teaching_notes: Predict first: a matchbox is a solid. How many faces does it have, and how many corners? Count every one only once. A face is a flat side of a solid. The box has 6 faces, and all of them are rectangles. Opposite faces are the same. A vertex is a point where faces meet. It is the corner of the solid. At every vertex of the box, 3 faces meet. Count the vertices the same way, ticking each one once. The box has 8 vertices. Models of solids such as the icosahedron and the dodecahedron can be made from nets, or built from straws and clay. You count their faces and vertices in the same way. Rule: count face by face and tick each one; a vertex is a point where faces meet. 1. Hold the box and tick each face once: top, bottom, front, back, left and right. 2. That makes 6 faces. Every face is a rectangle, and opposite faces are the same. 3. Look at one corner. A vertex is a point where faces meet. At this vertex 3 faces meet: the top, the front and the right. 4. Every vertex of the box looks the same, so 3 faces meet at every vertex. 5. Count the vertices: 4 on the top face and 4 on the bottom face, so 4 + 4 = 8. 6. Check: ticking each face and each vertex once gives 6 faces and 8 vertices, with none missed and none counted twice. Answer: The box has 6 faces, all rectangles. 3 faces meet at every vertex, and it has 8 vertices
